lists.title: Korean A1 Grammar Path
lists.description: First Korean: topic, subject, and object particles, the verb-last sentence, the copula, polite present and past, negation with 안, place particles 에/에서, question words, having with 있어요/없어요, counters, and linking with 하고/도.

lists.title: Korean A2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Getting things done: the 을 거예요 future, wanting with 고 싶어요, honorific requests with (으)세요, favours with 아/어 주세요, 못 vs 안, ability with (으)ㄹ 수 있어요, reasons with 아/어서, contrast with 지만, purpose with (으)러, and comparisons with 보다.

lists.title: Korean B1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Real sentences: the formal ㅂ니다 style, the ㅂ/ㄷ/르 irregular families, conditions with (으)면, command-friendly reasons with (으)니까, obligation and permission, noun-modifying clauses, ongoing and resulting states, and (으)ㄹ 때.

lists.title: Korean B2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Nuance: intention and inference with 겠, reported speech with 다고/라고, the 이히리기 passive and causative families, scene-setting with (으)ㄴ/는데, hedging with 것 같아요, and formal causes with 기 때문에.

lists.title: Korean C1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Register control: the full honorific machinery (께서, 시, humble 드리다/뵙다) and the plain written 한다-style of books and news.

lists.title: Korean C2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Native texture: squeezed quotations (대요/래요/냬요/재요) and the formal written connectives (으)며, (으)나, (으)므로.

points.title: Topic particle 은/는 (저는, 이것은)
points.function: Marks what the sentence is ABOUT: 는 after a vowel, 은 after a consonant
points.explanation: Korean tags the topic of a sentence with 은/는: 저는 학생이에요 (as for me, I'm a student). Use 는 when the word ends in a vowel (저는, 친구는) and 은 when it ends in a consonant (이것은, 선생님은). The topic is the frame — 'as for X' — and once set, you can drop it entirely in the next sentences.

points.title: Subject particle 이/가 (친구가, 물이)
points.function: Marks WHO or WHAT does it: 가 after a vowel, 이 after a consonant
points.explanation: 이/가 marks the grammatical subject — the one doing or being: 친구가 와요 (a friend is coming). 가 follows vowels (친구가), 이 follows consonants (물이). Against 은/는: use 이/가 for NEW information and answers to 'who?' (누가 왔어요? 친구가 왔어요), and 은/는 for what's already the topic.

points.title: Object particle 을/를 and verb-last order (밥을 먹어요)
points.function: Marks the thing acted on; the verb always comes LAST
points.explanation: Korean sentences end with the verb: subject – object – verb. The object wears 을/를: 밥을 먹어요 (I eat rice — literally 'rice-OBJECT eat'). 를 follows vowels (커피를), 을 follows consonants (밥을). Because the particles say who does what, word order before the verb is flexible — but the verb stays at the end.

points.title: The copula 이에요/예요 (책이에요, 의사예요)
points.function: 'X is Y': 이에요 after a consonant, 예요 after a vowel
points.explanation: To say 'X is Y', attach the copula straight to the noun: 책이에요 (it's a book), 의사예요 (she's a doctor). 이에요 follows consonants, 예요 follows vowels. The negative is a separate word with 이/가: 학생이 아니에요 (is not a student).

points.title: Present polite 아요/어요 (가요, 먹어요)
points.function: The everyday polite ending: 아요 after bright vowels ㅏ/ㅗ, 어요 otherwise
points.explanation: Drop 다 from the dictionary form and add 아요 or 어요: 가다 → 가요 (go), 먹다 → 먹어요 (eat). If the stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, use 아요 (살다 → 살아요); otherwise 어요 (읽다 → 읽어요). 하다 verbs become 해요 (공부하다 → 공부해요). This one form covers 'I go', 'she goes', and 'we go' — Korean verbs never change for person.

points.title: Negation with 안 (안 가요)
points.function: Put 안 right before the verb: don't / doesn't
points.explanation: The simplest negative is 안 in front of the verb: 안 가요 (I don't go), 안 먹어요 (I don't eat). With 하다 verbs, 안 slips between the noun and 하다: 공부 안 해요 (I don't study). The longer twin 지 않아요 means the same and sounds a touch more formal: 가지 않아요.

points.title: Place and time: 에 vs 에서 (집에, 집에서)
points.function: 에 = at/to (destination, time, existence); 에서 = where an action happens
points.explanation: 에 marks a destination or a time: 학교에 가요 (go TO school), 세 시에 (AT three o'clock), and where something simply exists: 집에 있어요 (be at home). 에서 marks where an ACTION happens: 집에서 공부해요 (study AT home). Rule of thumb: doing something somewhere → 에서; going somewhere or just being there → 에.

points.title: Past tense 았어요/었어요 (갔어요, 먹었어요)
points.function: Add 았/었 before 어요: bright-vowel stems take 았, the rest 었
points.explanation: The past slots 았/었 between stem and ending: 가다 → 갔어요 (went), 먹다 → 먹었어요 (ate). Bright vowels ㅏ/ㅗ take 았어요 (살았어요), everything else 었어요 (읽었어요), and 하다 becomes 했어요 (공부했어요). Same form for I/you/she/we — person never matters.

points.title: Question words: 뭐, 누구, 어디, 언제 (뭐 해요?)
points.function: Questions keep normal word order — just add the question word and a rising tone
points.explanation: Korean questions don't rearrange anything: 뭐 해요? (what are you doing?), 어디에 가요? (where are you going?). The polite ending 요 plus rising intonation is the whole question machinery. Who = 누구 (누가 as subject), what = 뭐/무엇, where = 어디, when = 언제, why = 왜, how = 어떻게.

points.title: 있어요/없어요: existing and having (시간이 있어요)
points.function: One pair covers 'there is / I have' and 'there isn't / I don't have'
points.explanation: 있어요 says something exists or you have it: 시간이 있어요 (I have time / there is time). 없어요 is its negative: 돈이 없어요 (I have no money). The thing possessed takes 이/가, not 을/를 — Korean literally says 'to me, time exists'. For people you respect, 있다 upgrades to 계시다: 할머니가 집에 계세요.

points.title: Counters: 개, 명, 마리 with native numbers (사과 두 개)
points.function: Count things as NOUN + number + counter, with the native numbers
points.explanation: Korean counts with measure words: 사과 두 개 (apples, two-item = two apples), 학생 세 명 (three students), 고양이 한 마리 (one cat). The pattern is noun + native number + counter. Before a counter, the first numbers shorten: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네. 개 counts objects, 명 people (분 politely), 마리 animals, 권 books, 잔 cups.

points.title: Linking nouns: 하고 (and/with) and 도 (also)
points.function: 하고 joins nouns or means 'together with'; 도 replaces 은/는/이/가 to say 'too'
points.explanation: 하고 glues nouns together: 빵하고 우유 (bread and milk), and doubles as 'with': 친구하고 갔어요 (I went with a friend). Its formal twins are 와 (after vowels) and 과 (after consonants). 도 means 'also/too' and REPLACES the topic or subject particle instead of stacking on it: 저도 가요 (I'm going too — never 저는도).

points.title: Future with (으)ㄹ 거예요 (갈 거예요)
points.function: Plans and predictions: stem + ㄹ/을 거예요
points.explanation: The everyday future: 내일 갈 거예요 (I'll go tomorrow). Vowel stems take ㄹ 거예요 (가다 → 갈 거예요), consonant stems take 을 거예요 (먹다 → 먹을 거예요). It covers both plans (I'm going to…) and guesses about the present: 지금 집에 있을 거예요 (he's probably home now).

points.title: Wanting: 고 싶어요 (가고 싶어요)
points.function: stem + 고 싶어요 = want to; third person uses 고 싶어해요
points.explanation: Attach 고 싶어요 to any verb stem: 한국에 가고 싶어요 (I want to go to Korea), 쉬고 싶어요 (I want to rest). The stem never changes — no vowel matching. For what SOMEONE ELSE wants, Korean switches to 고 싶어해요: 동생이 자고 싶어해요 (my sibling wants to sleep).

points.title: Polite requests and honorific (으)세요 (앉으세요)
points.function: One ending, two jobs: honoring the subject, and gentle commands
points.explanation: (으)세요 does double duty. As a request: 앉으세요 (please sit), 여기 보세요 (look here). As an honorific statement about someone respected: 할머니가 주무세요 (grandmother is sleeping — 자다 upgrades to 주무시다). Vowel stems take 세요 (가세요), consonant stems 으세요 (앉으세요). Some verbs swap entirely: 먹다 → 드세요, 자다 → 주무세요, 있다 → 계세요.

points.title: Do it for me: 아/어 주세요 (도와주세요)
points.function: Verb + 아/어 주세요 asks someone to do something FOR you
points.explanation: 주다 (to give) after another verb turns it into a favour: 문을 열어 주세요 (please open the door — literally 'open-give'). Bright stems take 아 주세요 (사 주세요 — buy for me), the rest 어 주세요 (읽어 주세요 — read for me). Statements work too: 친구가 도와줬어요 (a friend helped me out).

points.title: Can't: 못 vs won't: 안 (못 가요)
points.function: 안 = choose not to; 못 = unable to
points.explanation: 안 가요 means I'm not going (my choice); 못 가요 means I CAN'T go (something stops me). 못 sits right before the verb, and with 하다 verbs slips inside: 수영 못 해요 (I can't swim). The longer form is 지 못해요: 먹지 못해요. Pick by asking: is it refusal (안) or inability (못)?

points.title: Ability: (으)ㄹ 수 있어요/없어요 (할 수 있어요)
points.function: stem + ㄹ/을 수 있어요 = can; 없어요 = cannot
points.explanation: The full 'can' pattern: 한국어를 할 수 있어요 (I can speak Korean). Build the same stem as the future (가다 → 갈, 먹다 → 먹을), add 수 있어요 for can and 수 없어요 for cannot. 못 and (으)ㄹ 수 없어요 overlap — 못 is shorter and more spoken, this one is clearer and works in writing.

points.title: Because / and then: 아서/어서 (배가 고파서)
points.function: Links a reason or a sequence; never takes past tense before it
points.explanation: 아서/어서 chains clauses two ways. Reason: 배가 고파서 밥을 먹었어요 (I was hungry, so I ate). Sequence where the first step leads into the second: 친구를 만나서 영화를 봤어요 (I met a friend and [with them] watched a movie). The tense lives at the END only — never 갔어서. It can't order anyone around: no commands after 어서 (that's 으니까's job).

points.title: But and and: 지만, 고 (춥지만, 먹고)
points.function: 지만 = but; 고 = and (between clauses); both attach straight to the stem
points.explanation: 지만 contrasts: 춥지만 갈 거예요 (it's cold, but I'll go). 고 simply lists or sequences: 밥을 먹고 커피를 마셔요 (I eat, and [then] drink coffee). Both glue onto the plain stem of any verb — no vowel matching. Unlike 어서, 고 allows past before it in lists: 어제는 일했고 오늘은 쉬어요.

points.title: Going somewhere to do: (으)러 가요 (먹으러 가요)
points.function: stem + (으)러 + a motion verb = go/come in order to
points.explanation: For purpose plus movement: 밥을 먹으러 가요 (I'm going [somewhere] to eat), 친구를 만나러 왔어요 (I came to meet a friend). Vowel stems take 러 (보러), consonant stems 으러 (먹으러). It ONLY works with motion verbs like 가다/오다/다니다 — for other purposes Korean uses (으)려고.

points.title: Comparing: 보다 and 제일/가장 (더 커요)
points.function: X보다 (더) = more than X; 제일/가장 = the most
points.explanation: Comparison hangs 보다 on the loser: 형은 저보다 커요 (my brother is taller than me). 더 (more) is optional but common: 저보다 더 커요. For superlatives put 제일 or 가장 before the describing word: 제일 좋아요 (like it the most), 가장 큰 도시 (the biggest city). Less = 덜.

points.title: Formal style ㅂ니다/습니다 (감사합니다)
points.function: News-and-business polite: ㅂ니다 after vowels, 습니다 after consonants
points.explanation: The formal register of announcements, presentations, and shops: 감사합니다 (thank you), 알겠습니다 (understood). Vowel stems fuse ㅂ into the last syllable + 니다 (가다 → 갑니다), consonant stems add 습니다 (먹다 → 먹습니다). Questions swap 다 for 까: 어디에 갑니까? Everyday conversation stays in 요-form; this style signals distance and respect.

points.title: Irregular verbs: ㅂ, ㄷ, 르 (추워요, 들어요, 몰라요)
points.function: Three stem families that transform before vowel endings
points.explanation: Some stems shapeshift before 아/어. ㅂ-irregulars melt ㅂ into 우: 춥다 → 추워요 (cold), 돕다 → 도와요 (help). ㄷ-irregulars soften ㄷ to ㄹ: 듣다 → 들어요 (listen), 걷다 → 걸어요 (walk). 르-irregulars double the ㄹ: 모르다 → 몰라요 (not know), 빠르다 → 빨라요 (fast). Before consonant endings they behave: 춥지만, 듣고, 모르지만.

points.title: If and when: (으)면 (시간이 있으면)
points.function: stem + 면/으면 covers both 'if' and 'when(ever)'
points.explanation: One ending for conditions and habitual whens: 시간이 있으면 오세요 (come if you have time), 봄이 오면 꽃이 펴요 (when spring comes, flowers bloom). Vowel stems take 면 (가면), consonant stems 으면 (먹으면). 만약 up front flags a pure hypothesis: 만약 비가 오면… (if it should rain…).

points.title: Because (commands allowed): (으)니까 (늦으니까)
points.function: The reason connector that CAN introduce commands and suggestions
points.explanation: (으)니까 gives a reason like 어서, with two differences: it happily precedes commands and let's-suggestions — 늦으니까 빨리 가세요 (it's late, so hurry) — and it can carry past tense: 어제 갔으니까 오늘은 안 가요 (since I went yesterday, I'm not going today). 어서 can do neither. For apologies and thanks, though, Korean insists on 어서: 늦어서 미안해요.

points.title: Must and may: 아/어야 해요, 아/어도 돼요 (가야 해요)
points.function: 야 해요 = have to; 도 돼요 = it's okay to; (으)면 안 돼요 = must not
points.explanation: Obligation: verb + 아/어야 해요 — 지금 가야 해요 (I have to go now). Permission: 아/어도 돼요 — 여기 앉아도 돼요? (may I sit here?). Prohibition flips to (으)면 안 돼요 — 여기서 담배를 피우면 안 돼요 (you must not smoke here). The three form the classroom-and-real-life triangle of rules.

points.title: Describing nouns: 는/(으)ㄴ/(으)ㄹ (읽는 책)
points.function: Whole clauses become noun modifiers — Korean's relative clauses, always BEFORE the noun
points.explanation: 'The book I'm reading' turns around in Korean: 제가 읽는 책 (I-read book). Verbs take 는 for present (읽는 책), (으)ㄴ for past (읽은 책 — the book I read), (으)ㄹ for future (읽을 책 — the book I'll read). Descriptive verbs use (으)ㄴ for their plain present: 큰 집 (a big house), 예쁜 꽃 (a pretty flower). No word for 'who/which/that' — position does everything.

points.title: Ongoing and resulting: 고 있어요 / 아·어 있어요 (자고 있어요)
points.function: 고 있어요 = in the middle of doing; 아/어 있어요 = in the state that resulted
points.explanation: 고 있어요 is the -ing of action in progress: 지금 밥을 먹고 있어요 (I'm eating right now). 아/어 있어요 is for the STATE left after an action: 문이 열려 있어요 (the door stands open), 앉아 있어요 (is seated). Honor the subject by upgrading 있다: 선생님이 기다리고 계세요.

points.title: When: (으)ㄹ 때 (먹을 때, 어렸을 때)
points.function: stem + ㄹ/을 때 = at the time of doing/being
points.explanation: 때 (time) after the future-modifier stem means 'when': 밥을 먹을 때 (when eating), 학교에 갈 때 (when going to school). For a finished past, 았/었을 때: 어렸을 때 (when I was young), 한국에 살았을 때 (when I lived in Korea). Nouns take 때 directly: 시험 때 (at exam time), 방학 때 (during vacation).

points.title: Intention and guessing with 겠 (하겠습니다, 맛있겠다)
points.function: First person: I will (resolve); elsewhere: must be / looks like
points.explanation: 겠 slides in before the ending and changes meaning by person. On yourself it's commitment: 제가 하겠습니다 (I'll do it). About anything else it's an on-the-spot inference: 맛있겠어요 (that looks delicious), 힘들겠어요 (that must be tough), 내일은 춥겠습니다 (tomorrow will be cold — the weather-forecast future). Set phrases live here too: 알겠습니다, 모르겠어요.

drills.hint: 하다 + the resolve marker, formal

drills.translation: Wow, that looks really delicious!
drills.hint: 맛있다 + the looks-like marker

points.title: Reported speech: 다고/라고 해요 (온다고 해요)
points.function: Fold what someone said into your sentence with 다고 (verbs) / 라고 (nouns)
points.explanation: To relay speech, quote the PLAIN form + 고 하다: 친구가 내일 온다고 해요 (my friend says he's coming tomorrow). Action verbs in present take ㄴ/는다고 (간다고, 먹는다고), descriptive verbs keep 다고 (바쁘다고), nouns take (이)라고 (학생이라고 해요 — says he's a student). Past adds 았/었다고. It's also how Korean names things: 이것을 김치라고 해요 (this is called kimchi).

drills.hint: 오다 in the quoted plain form + 고

points.title: Passive and causative: 이히리기 (열리다, 먹이다)
points.function: One suffix family, two directions: be-done-to (passive) and make-do (causative)
points.explanation: Korean derives both voices with the 이/히/리/기 suffixes — which verb takes which is memorized, not computed. Passive: 열다 → 열리다 (be opened: 문이 열렸어요), 듣다 → 들리다 (be heard: 소리가 들려요), 보다 → 보이다 (be visible: 산이 보여요). Causative: 먹다 → 먹이다 (feed), 입다 → 입히다 (dress someone), 자다 → 재우다 (put to sleep). The catch-all causative is 게 하다: 웃게 해요 (makes me laugh).

points.title: Background and contrast: (으)ㄴ/는데 (바쁜데, 가는데)
points.function: Sets the scene, contrasts, or softens — Korean's favourite clause glue
points.explanation: 은데/는데 frames what follows: 지금 바쁜데 나중에 전화해도 돼요? (I'm busy right now — can I call later?). Action verbs take 는데 (가는데, 먹는데), descriptive verbs (으)ㄴ데 (바쁜데, 추운데), nouns 인데. It contrasts (형은 큰데 저는 작아요), introduces background before a request, and trails off politely on its own: 좀 비싼데요… (it's a bit pricey…).

points.function: Hedge anything: modifier form + 것 같아요 = it seems / I think
points.explanation: Korean softens claims with 것 같아요 after the noun-modifier forms: 비가 올 것 같아요 (it looks like rain — future ㄹ), 자는 것 같아요 (he seems to be sleeping — present 는), 벌써 간 것 같아요 (seems she already left — past ㄴ). Koreans also use it for polite opinions where English would be direct: 좀 매운 것 같아요 (I find it a bit spicy).

points.title: Because, formally: 기 때문에 (일 때문에)
points.function: Noun/stem + 때문에 pins the cause; heavier than 아서 or 으니까
points.explanation: 때문에 hangs off a noun (일 때문에 못 가요 — I can't go because of work) or a nominalized verb with 기 (비가 오기 때문에 — because it is raining). It states causes with written-register weight; conversation prefers 어서/으니까. Blame or credit a WHOLE clause with 았기/었기 때문에 for past causes. Related: 덕분에 (thanks to) for good causes, 때문에 alone can sound accusatory.

points.title: Honorific machinery: 께서, 드리다, 뵙다 (선생님께서 말씀하셨어요)
points.function: Raising the subject (께서 + 시) and lowering yourself (humble verbs)
points.explanation: Full honorific Korean works both directions. Raise the respected subject: 이/가 becomes 께서, 에게 becomes 께, and the verb takes 시 — 선생님께서 말씀하셨어요 (the teacher spoke). Lower yourself with humble verbs: 주다 → 드리다 (give TO a superior), 만나다 → 뵙다 (meet a superior), 말하다 → 말씀드리다, 묻다 → 여쭤보다. The choreography: honor THEM with 시, humble YOURSELF with 드리다-verbs — never 시 on your own actions.

points.title: Irregular Stems + ~ㄹ/을
points.function: Attach the future/modifier ending ~ㄹ/을 correctly to irregular verbs and adjectives.
points.explanation: ㅅ, ㄷ and ㅂ irregulars change as usual when a vowel-initial addition is attached (짓다 → 지을, 걷다 → 걸을, 쉽다 → 쉬울, 돕다 → 도울; note 돕다 becomes 도우- because ㅂ becomes 오 only before ~아/어). ㅡ and 르 irregulars are unaffected (잠그다 → 잠글, 다르다 → 다를). Stems ending in ㄹ drop that ㄹ and reattach ~ㄹ, so the form looks unchanged (길다 → 길, 갈다 → 갈, 빨다 → 빨, 열다 → 열). Regular consonant stems simply take ~을 (잃다 → 잃을) and regular vowel stems take ~ㄹ (예쁘다 → 예쁠). The same changes happen with any addition beginning in ~ㄹ/을, such as ~ㄹ/을래(요), ~ㄹ/을까(요), ~ㄹ/을게(요), ~ㄹ/을걸(요).

points.explanation: 되다 means 'to become'; the noun the subject becomes takes ~이/가, not ~를/을 (저는 선생님이 되었어요 = I became a teacher). Because it is awkward to say 이겠다, the future 'will be' is normally expressed with ~ㄹ/을 것이다 on 이다 (선생님일 것이다) or with 되다 (선생님이 될 것이다), which are practically the same in meaning. The 일 in 선생님일 거예요 is not the word 일 — it is 이다 + ~ㄹ. For negatives, 되다 takes 안 or ~지 않다 (되지 않을 거야), while an 이다 sentence uses 아니다 (아닐 거야).

points.title: Pure Korean Numbers and Counters
points.function: Count things, people and actions with pure Korean numbers plus a counter.
points.explanation: Pure Korean numbers are 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷, 다섯, 여섯, 일곱, 여덟, 아홉, 열, 스물, 서른, 마흔, 쉰 (and 예순 for 60, rarely used). Teens and higher combinations simply stack the words: 열하나 (11), 열둘 (12), 스물하나 (21), 쉰아홉 (59), with no space inside the number. Pure Korean numbers are used for counting things/people/actions, for the hour, and sometimes for months. When counting you normally need a counter: 개 (things), 명 (people), 번 (actions); 개 can substitute if you forget a specific counter. The pattern is noun + number + counter (사람 두 명, 펜 다섯 개); the alternative number + counter + ~의 + noun (두 명의 사람) is much less common. Before a counter, 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무. A space is written between the number word and the counter (한 개, 두 번, 세 명).
points.culture_note: English rarely uses counters ('two rolls of film' is one of the few cases), while Korean uses them to count nearly everything.

points.title: Counters with numbers (개, 명, 대, 잔)
points.function: Count nouns in a sentence using a number plus a counter.
points.explanation: The usual order is noun + number + counter, and the particle (를/을, 가/이) attaches to the counter: 나는 펜 네 개를 샀어. The number-counter combination can also be moved in front of the noun with ~의: 나는 네 개의 펜을 샀어. In speech the particle is often dropped altogether (펜 네 개 샀어), and it is also possible to attach the particle to the noun instead of the counter (펜을 네 개 샀어). All three versions sound perfectly natural to Korean speakers. Pure Korean numbers are used with these counters, and 하나/둘/셋/넷 shorten to 한/두/세/네 before a counter. When a pure Korean number is used with a counter, the number is usually written out as a word rather than as a numeral, with a space before the counter.

points.title: Telling time: 시 and 분
points.function: Tell the time on a clock and say when something happens.
points.explanation: Put 시 after a number for the hour and 분 after a number for the minutes: 2 시 30 분 = 2:30. The hour takes pure Korean numbers (두 시, 세 시, 열두 시) while the minutes take Sino-Korean numbers (삼십 분, 오십 분). If you spell the number out as a word, leave a space before the counter (두 시, 삼십 분); if you use a numeral, it is acceptable either to keep or omit the space (2 시 30 분 / 2시 30분). To say when something happens, add 에 to the time: 나는 5 시에 먹을 거야.

points.title: Age with 살
points.function: State and ask someone's age.
points.explanation: Use pure Korean numbers with the counter 살: 저는 열 살이에요 (I am ten years old), 스물여섯 살이에요 (twenty-six years old). Using Sino-Korean numbers sounds strange under thirty, but after thirty it is not unusual, and above fifty Sino-Korean numbers are what you will normally hear. A very common question worth memorising is (나이가) 몇 살이에요? = How old are you?

points.title: 번째: ordinal numbers
points.function: Say first, second, third, fourth… before a noun.
points.explanation: 번째 is attached after a number like a counter to make an ordinal. For 'first', 첫 replaces 한: 첫 번째. Just as with other counters, 2–4 use the short forms 두/세/네: 두 번째, 세 번째, 네 번째. From five upwards the number does not change: 열 번째 (tenth), 백 번째 (100th).

points.title: Shortened ordinals: 첫째, 둘째, 셋째, 넷째
points.function: Use the short ordinal forms for one's children and for listing points.
points.explanation: 첫 번째 = 첫째, 두 번째 = 둘째, 세 번째 = 셋째, 네 번째 = 넷째, etc. These short forms cannot be used in as many situations as the longer ones. They are most common when talking about one's first/second/third child (우리 둘째 아들 = our second son, or simply 우리 둘째 = our second (child)), and when enumerating points in a list (첫째, … 둘째, … = firstly…, secondly…). They also work with 날 (둘째 날 = the second day).

drills.hint: short ordinal for the number one

drills.hint: short ordinal used to open a list

points.title: 마지막 (final) vs 지난 (previous)
points.function: Distinguish the two Korean equivalents of English 'last'.
points.explanation: 마지막 refers to the final thing at the end of a sequence (the last meal of the day, the last week of a trip). It never means 'previous'; for that, 지난 is used. Although 마지막 is used before a noun like a descriptive word, it is not an adjective (it does not end in 다 and cannot be conjugated) — compare English 'face paint', where a noun describes a noun. So 마지막 수업 = the final class, but 지난 수업 = the previous class.

drills.translation: This is my last (final) class.
drills.hint: the final item at the end of a sequence

drills.translation: I didn't see the last one.
drills.hint: the final item of a series

drills.hint: the one before this one

drills.hint: the bus at the end of the run, with none after it

drills.hint: the train that closes the day's service — not the train before this one

drills.hint: the exam before this one; nothing here is about the end of a series

drills.hint: the semester before this one, not the final semester of the course

points.title: 처음 – at first / for the first time
points.function: Talk about the beginning of something or about doing something for the first time.
points.explanation: 처음 can behave as a noun or an adverb. (1) 처음에 … means 'at first / in the beginning': 처음에 그 여자를 싫어했어요. (2) Placed in a sentence as an adverb, it says that this is the first time something happens: 저는 어제 선생님을 처음 만났어요 (I met my teacher for the first time yesterday).

drills.hint: the beginning stage, plus 에

drills.hint: adverb meaning for the very first occasion

drills.hint: adverb: that meeting was the earliest one, never before

drills.hint: the earliest stage of the situation — the 'back then' that 지금 is set against

drills.hint: adverb asking whether this visit is the earliest one — never been before

drills.translation: This is my first time in Korea.
drills.hint: used as a noun here, with 이에요: an occasion that has never happened before

drills.translation: My younger sibling rode a bicycle for the first time yesterday.
drills.hint: adverb: yesterday was the earliest time he had ever done it

points.title: 동안 – 'for' a period of time
points.function: Say how long an action lasts.
points.explanation: 동안 is placed after a duration: 2 분 동안 (for 2 minutes), 이틀 동안 (for two days), 세 시간 동안 (for three hours). No particle is added after 동안 — learners expect 에, but it is not used. Literally you are saying 'for that period of time': 저는 30 분 동안 공부했어요 = I studied for (a period of) 30 minutes. (동안 can later also mean 'while' another action occurs.) Spacing: if the number is written as a word, leave a space (십 분 동안); with a numeral, a space is optional.

drills.hint: marks the length of the period

drills.hint: marks the length of the period

drills.hint: marks the length of the period

drills.hint: goes straight after the length of the stay; learners wrongly add 에 to it

drills.hint: follows the stated length to say how long the watching lasts

drills.translation: It rained for two hours yesterday.
drills.hint: placed after the two-hour stretch to say how long the rain kept up

points.title: Counting hours: 시간 vs 시
points.function: Distinguish the hour on the clock from an amount of hours.
points.explanation: 시 is used for the hour on a clock (3 시 = 3:00, 세 시 = three o'clock), while 시간 counts hours as a duration (3 시간 동안 = for three hours). Pure Korean numbers are used with both. 시간 also means 'time' in general, which is why 지난 시간 means 'last time' and 다음 시간 means 'next time'.

drills.hint: unit for an amount of hours

drills.hint: unit for a duration in hours

drills.hint: unit for a duration in hours

drills.hint: unit for the hour shown on a clock

points.title: Counting seconds: 초
points.function: Count seconds of time.
points.explanation: 초 (second) is counted with Sino-Korean numbers, and it makes no difference whether you write the numeral or the word: 1 초 / 일 초, 2 초 / 이 초, 2 초 동안 / 이 초 동안 (for two seconds).

drills.hint: unit smaller than a minute

drills.hint: unit counted with Sino-Korean numbers; sixty of them make a minute

drills.hint: the smallest unit shown on a game clock

drills.hint: unit of the countdown before the shutter goes

drills.hint: one of these is a sixtieth of a minute

points.title: 지난/다음 + time words (last time / next time)
points.function: Refer to the previous or the following week, month, class or occasion.
points.explanation: 지난 is placed immediately before some time words to mean 'previous/last': 지난 주, 지난 달, 지난 수업. 다음 works the same way for 'next': 다음 주, 다음 달. 지난 cannot be used with very short units (지난 분/지난 초 are impossible). Because 시간 also means 'time', 지난 시간 and 다음 시간 mean 'last time' and 'next time' (never 'last/next hour'); 지난 번 and 다음 번 are used the same way. Note that 'to attend a class' is 수업을 듣다 (literally 'to listen to a class'), so the object particle ~을 is used, not ~에.

drills.hint: the previous one

drills.translation: I will go to Canada next week.
drills.hint: the following one

drills.hint: occasion word used after 지난

drills.hint: word meaning both 'time' and hours

drills.hint: goes straight in front of a time word for 'previous'; before 시간 it points to the earlier occasion, not the earlier hour

drills.translation: Do you have time next month?
drills.hint: goes in front of a time word for the one that comes after this one

points.title: Korean days: 일, 날, 하루
points.function: Count days, name a date, and refer to a specific day.
points.explanation: 일 means 'day' but is never used alone (alone it means 'work'); it appears inside day names such as 총선일 or 현충일. As the counter for days it takes Sino-Korean numbers, and the numeral or the word are equally fine: 3 일 동안 = 삼 일 동안 (for three days). There are also native words for small numbers of days — 하루 (one day, far more common than 일 일), 이틀 (two days), 사흘 (three days) — but from two days up the Sino-Korean forms (이 일, 삼 일, 사 일…) are used more. A Sino-Korean number + 일 also names a date, and context makes the two uses clear: 3 일에 (on the 3rd) vs 3 일 동안 (for three days). Dates combine #월 and #일: 3 월 2 일 = March 2nd. 날 is another word for 'day' that stands alone but cannot be counted: 그 날에 = on that day. With 날 you can use ordinals (두 번째 날 / 둘째 날 = the second day), and 첫날 specifically means 'the first day'.

drills.hint: counter for days, with Sino-Korean numbers

points.function: Count weeks and talk about last/next week.
points.explanation: 주 (week) is used with Sino-Korean numbers, and the numeral or the word are both fine: 2 주 동안 = 이 주 동안 (for two weeks). 주일 can also be used as a counter for weeks (2 주일 동안), but 주 sounds slightly more natural. Combined with 지난/다음: 지난 주에, 다음 주에.

points.title: Korean months: 달 vs 개월
points.function: Count months of duration with the right number system.
points.explanation: Both 달 and 개월 mean 'month' when counting, with no difference in meaning; both are frequent. 달 is a native Korean word and takes pure Korean numbers (두 달), while 개월 is of Chinese origin and takes Sino-Korean numbers (이 개월 / 2 개월). With 달 the number is usually written as a word; with 개월 the numeral or the word are both fine. Strictly speaking, the sense of 'for a period' is already inside 달, but most people still add 동안 after it.

points.title: Month names (1월 – 12월)
points.function: Name the months of the calendar.
points.explanation: The names of the months are simply the Sino-Korean number of the month + 월: 1 월 (일월) = January, 2 월 (이월) = February … 12 월 (십이월) = December. Two readings are irregular: 6 월 is 유월 (not 육월) and 10 월 is 시월 (not 십월). A date is given as #월 #일: 3 월 2 일 = March 2nd.

points.title: Pure Korean vs Sino-Korean numbers with time counters
points.function: Decide which number system a time word takes.
points.explanation: The choice is not random: whenever the time word is of Chinese origin, Sino-Korean numbers are used; native Korean time words take pure Korean numbers. That is why 개월 (month) is counted 이 개월 while native 달 is counted 두 달. Pure Korean: 시 (o'clock), 시간 (hours), 달 (months), 살 (age), 번 (times), and counters like 개, 명, 대, 잔. Sino-Korean: 분 (minutes), 초 (seconds), 일 (days), 주/주일 (weeks), 개월 (months), 월 (calendar months). When a pure Korean number is used with a counter, the word is usually written out; with Sino-Korean numbers the numeral and the word are equally acceptable.

points.title: Passive verbs with ~아/어 있다 (describing a state)
points.function: Say that something is currently in a resulting state (on, off, open, closed, locked) rather than that an event happened.
points.explanation: Take a passive verb (켜지다, 꺼지다, 잠기다, 닫히다…), attach ~아/어 to the stem and add 있다: 켜져 있다, 꺜져 있다 → 꺼져 있다, 잠겨 있다, 닫혀 있다. The subject of such a sentence normally takes ~이/가, not ~은/는 or ~을/를, because a passive verb can never act on an object. Compare: 문이 닫혔어요 (at some point the door got closed — an event) vs 문이 닫혀 있어요 (right now the door is in the state of closed). All three tenses exist for both readings: 닫혔어요 / 닫혀 있었어요, 닫혀요 / 닫혀 있어요, 닫힐 거예요 / 닫혀 있을 거예요. ~아/어 있다 is only possible when the result of the verb is a lasting state; it does not work with verbs like 속다 (once you are tricked, you are simply tricked, so 속아 있다 makes no sense).

points.title: Passive/active pairs with 나다 and 내다
points.function: Pair up verbs where 나다 gives the passive meaning and 내다 the active meaning.
points.explanation: Just like 하다 (active) / 되다 (passive), a word ending in 내다 is active and the same word ending in 나다 is passive: 끝내다 = to finish (something), 끝나다 = to be finished; 고장 내다 = to break (something), 고장 나다 = to be broken. Standing alone, 나다 means 'for something to come up/arise/occur' and 내다 means 'to make something come up/arise/occur'. Not every 나다 word has a 내다 partner (어긋나다 exists, 어긋내다 does not). With these pairs the past tense is normally used even when the situation is true right now: 숙제는 끝났어요 = my homework is finished; 컴퓨터는 고장 났어요 = the computer is broken. The active versions are possible but less common in these cases.

points.title: 나다 with nouns (기억이 나다, 화가 나다, 땀이 나다…)
points.function: Express that a memory, idea, smell, feeling or event 'comes up'.
points.explanation: Because 나다 means 'for something to come up/arise', it combines with many nouns, and the noun always takes ~이/가 (never ~을/를) since 나다 is passive: 기억이 나다 (to remember), 생각이 나다 (an idea comes to mind), 냄새가 나다 (to smell), 소리가 나다 (a sound occurs), 화가 나다 (to be angry), 사고가 나다 (to get in an accident), 땀이 나다 (to sweat), 전쟁이 나다 (for a war to break out), 멀미가 나다 (to get motion sick). These expressions are usually put in the past tense where English uses the present, because the thing has already 'come up': 땀이 났어요 = I'm sweating. The present tense means it is coming up at this very moment: 땀이 나요 = sweat is literally coming out right now. In negative sentences this past-for-present effect disappears: 나는 그것이 기억 안 나 = I don't remember that (present), while 그때 기억이 안 났어 refers to the past.
points.culture_note: 큰 일 났어요! literally 'a big thing came up' is used like 'Oh no!' / 'Oh crap!'.

points.title: Turning adjectives into verbs with ~아/어하다 (좋아하다, 싫어하다)
points.function: Change an adjective describing a feeling into a verb that can take an object.
points.explanation: Attach ~아/어하다 to the stem of an adjective: 좋다 (to be good) → 좋아하다 (to like), 싫다 (to be not good) → 싫어하다 (to dislike). The result is a verb, so it takes the object particle ~을/를: 저는 김치를 좋아해요. Note that unlike most 하다 verbs you cannot strip off ~하다 to get a noun: 좋아 and 싫어 are not nouns — they only occur as conjugated forms of 좋다/싫다. Other adjectives work the same way: 부끄럽다 → 부끄러워하다, 부럽다 → 부러워하다.

points.title: The many uses of 들다
points.function: Understand 들다 through its two overarching meanings instead of one fixed translation.
points.explanation: 들다 has two broad senses: (1) to carry/hold/lift something — 저는 손을 들었어요 (I raised my hand), 저는 가방을 들었어요 (I carried the bag); and (2) to enter/go into something — 나는 동아리에 들었어 (I joined a club), 잠이 들었다 (I fell asleep, 'entered sleep'), 저는 그 그림이 마음에 들어요 (I like that picture, 'the picture enters my heart'). Rather than translating 들다 with a single English word, read the whole collocation and let context decide. 들다 also appears in many compound verbs (들어가다, 들어오다).

points.title: Comparing with 다르다/비슷하다/같다 and the particle ~와/과/랑/이랑/하고
points.function: Say that something is different from, similar to, or the same as something else.
points.explanation: 다르다 (different), 비슷하다 (similar) and 같다 (same) are adjectives and can predicate a sentence on their own (그것은 비슷해요). To name the thing being compared, Korean uses ONE particle family — ~와/과 (written/formal; 와 after a vowel, 과 after a consonant), ~랑/이랑 (casual; 랑 after a vowel, 이랑 after a consonant) or ~하고 — where English uses three different prepositions (different FROM, similar TO, the same AS). Word order can also be flipped so that both compared items are the subject: 저와 저의 친구는 비슷해요 ('Me and my friend are similar'), with no change in meaning. When nothing is actually being compared, 똑같다 ('exactly the same') is more natural than 같다.

points.title: Describing nouns with adjective phrases (다른/같은/비슷한)
points.function: Put an adjective — or a whole comparison phrase — in front of a noun to describe it.
points.explanation: Korean adjectives can modify a following noun: 하다-adjectives take ~한 (비슷한), 같다 becomes 같은, 다르다 becomes 다른. The pattern is Subject – adjective(describing) – object – verb: 나는 비슷한 남자를 만났어. Because the comparison particle phrase belongs to the adjective, the whole phrase can sit in front of the noun: (X와 비슷한) 남자 = 'a man who is similar to X'. This is an introduction to describing nouns with whole phrases rather than single adjectives. Note also that 다른 can mean 'other/another (a different one)', not only 'not the same'.

points.title: 또 다르다 = another (vs. 다르다 = other)
points.function: Point out one more item of a kind that has already been discussed.
points.explanation: 또 다르다 is not one word: it is the adverb 또 ('again') plus the adjective 다르다. 다르다 alone usually translates as 'other/a different one', while 또 다르다 translates as 'another' — used when one particular thing has already been described and you are adding one more. 저는 다른 영화를 봤어요 = I saw a different movie (instead of the planned one); 저는 또 다른 영화를 봤어요 = I saw ANother movie (I saw one, then saw a different one again).

points.title: 걸리다: one word, many meanings
points.function: Recognize and use the four common meanings of 걸리다.
points.explanation: Korean has many homonyms; 쓰다 (to write / to use / to wear a hat) is one, and 걸리다 is another. 걸리다 can mean: (1) to be in the state of hanging — usually with ~어 있다 (벽에 걸려 있어요); (2) to be caught/stuck/trapped (줄에 걸렸어); (3) to take an amount of time (두 시간 걸려요), often with A부터/에서 B까지; (4) to catch a cold or sickness, with the particle ~에 (감기에 걸렸어요). All four share the core nuance of being 'caught/stuck in' something, so try not to think of them as four unrelated words.

points.title: Talking about pain and sickness: 아프다 and ~에 걸리다
points.function: Say that a body part hurts, that you were sick, or that you caught a cold/flu.
points.explanation: 아프다 is an adjective covering both 'sick' and 'sore'. When you talk about a place on your body, the body part takes 이/가 (not 는/은): 배가 아파요, 팔이 아파요. For a person being sick, 저는 어제 너무 아팠어요. For illnesses you 'catch', use 걸리다 with the particle ~에: 저는 감기에 걸렸어요, 저는 독감에 걸렸어요 — and note that Korean uses the PAST 걸렸다 even when you currently have the cold. 기침 (a cough) and 재채기 (a sneeze) are nouns that take 하다 to become verbs (기침하다, 재채기하다).

points.title: Korean suffix: ~적/~적으로/~적이다
points.function: Turn certain Chinese-origin nouns into descriptive words, adverbs and adjectives.
points.explanation: ~적 (的) attaches to some nouns of Chinese origin and creates a word meaning 'relating to / having the properties of' that noun — usually English '-al' (문화 → 문화적 cultural), though not always (과학 → 과학적 'scientific', 충동 → 충동적 'impulsive'). There is no way to predict which nouns allow ~적; you have to learn each one. Adding ~으로 makes an adverb ('-ly'): 문화적으로 = culturally. Adding ~이다 makes an adjective that can predicate a sentence (충동적이에요) or, as ~적인, describe a following noun (역사적인 건물). ~적 by itself is still a noun, so nothing is conjugated (민주적 정부); ~적이다 must be conjugated like 이다. Both ~적 and ~적인 can modify a noun with the same meaning, but ~적인 is generally preferred, especially in speech; bare ~적 turns up more often in print.

points.title: Korean suffix: ~스럽다
points.function: Make an adjective meaning 'having the properties of' a noun.
points.explanation: ~스럽다 attaches to some nouns and creates an adjective, much like ~적이다: 사랑 (love) → 사랑스럽다 (lovely), 자연 (nature) → 자연스럽다 (natural), 실망 (disappointment) → 실망스럽다 (disappointing), 만족 (satisfaction) → 만족스럽다 (satisfactory). As with ~적, there is no way to predict which nouns accept ~스럽다, so each one appears as its own vocabulary entry. All ~스럽다 words are ㅂ-irregular adjectives: 사랑스럽다 → 사랑스러워요, and past 사랑스러웠어요. ~스럽다 is sometimes added to nouns that already have a 하다 form (실망하다), and the two are not interchangeable.

points.title: 실망하다 vs. 실망스럽다 (with ~에게/한테 and ~에)
points.function: Say you are disappointed, or that something is disappointing, with the right particles.
points.explanation: 실망하다 is a VERB describing someone's emotion of being disappointed: 저는 실망했어요. It cannot act on an object (like 자다 or 죽다), so to say who or what you are disappointed IN, attach ~에게/한테 to a person (저는 친구에게 실망했어요) and ~에 to a non-person (저는 영화에 실망했어요) — the same rule as with passive verbs. 실망스럽다, on the other hand, is an adjective describing the thing that is disappointing, and is used in the Subject–Object–Adjective pattern: 저는 친구가 실망스러워요 ('my friend is disappointing, so I'm disappointed'). 저는 실망스러워요 on its own simply omits that thing, and listeners will ask 'in what?'.

points.title: Adjectives with ~스럽다
points.function: Turn a noun into an adjective meaning 'having the properties of that noun'.
points.explanation: Adding ~스럽다 to a noun (실망, 만족, 사랑, 자랑, 자연) creates an adjective describing something that has the properties of that noun: 실망스럽다 = disappointing, 만족스럽다 = satisfactory, 사랑스럽다 = lovely, 자랑스럽다 = proud(-making), 자연스럽다 = natural. The ~하다 counterpart (실망하다, 만족하다, 사랑하다, 자랑하다) is a verb that describes a person's emotion or acts on an object, while the ~스럽다 form is an adjective describing the thing itself. ~스럽다 adjectives are frequently used in the Subject – Object – Adjective pattern (저는 결과가 만족스러웠어요 = I was satisfied with the results), and the object may be dropped (저는 만족스러웠어요). All ~스럽다 words are ㅂ-irregular adjectives (…스러워요, …스러웠어요) and can modify a following noun with ~ㄴ/은 → ~스러운.

points.explanation: Attach ~게 to the stem of a ~스럽다 adjective to turn it into an adverb describing how an action is done: 자연스럽게 (naturally), 사랑스럽게 (lovingly), 실망스럽게 (disappointingly), 만족스럽게 (satisfactorily). The adverb goes before the verb it modifies and can never be followed by 이다.

points.title: Sequential ~아/어서
points.function: Link two actions where the first is intrinsically connected to the second ('go and then …', 'sit and then …').
points.explanation: Attach ~아/어서 to the stem of the verb in the first clause. Unlike ~고, ~아/어서 is used when the first action is directly linked to the second — the second action depends on it. It is required with 가다 and 오다 when you go/come somewhere and then do something (학교에 가서 공부할 거예요, 집에 와서 바로 잤어요) and with the position verbs 앉다, 서다, 눕다 when you do something while in that position (누워서 책을 읽었어요, 앉아서 쉴 거야, 줄에 서서 순서를 기다렸어요). The verb before ~아/어서 is never conjugated to the past tense. It can also be used with other verbs whose action leads into the next (고기를 골라서 같이 먹었어요, 문을 열어서 밖으로 나갔어요). ~고 may still be used with 가다/오다 when merely listing similar ideas (혜원도 오고… 슬기도 오고…).

points.title: I want to: ~고 싶다
points.function: Say that you want to do an action.
points.explanation: Attach ~고 싶다 to a verb stem: 저는 캐나다에 가고 싶어요 = I want to go to Canada. It works with 되다 to mean 'want to become' (선생님이 되고 싶어요) and can be used in the past (되고 싶었어요). 싶다 behaves as an adjective and must be conjugated like one: 먹고 싶다 / 먹고 싶어요, never 먹고 싶는다. Negation is made with 안 before the verb (안 마시고 싶어요) or ~지 않다 on 싶다 (울고 싶지 않아요). ~고 싶다 is not used with adjectives — 'I want to be happy' needs ~아/어지다 ('become'). Compare 원하다, which is used for wanting a noun object (그 책을 원해요) versus ~고 싶다 for wanting to do something (그 책을 읽고 싶어요). 보고 싶다 literally 'want to see' is how you say you miss a person; 그립다 is used for missing non-persons.

points.title: ~이/가 and ~는/은 Revisited
points.function: Choose between the topic and subject particle: general fact vs. newly noticed specific situation.
points.explanation: Besides its comparison function, ~는/은 marks a general fact or statement: 로키 산은 높아요 (as a well-known general truth); 산은 높다 ≈ 'in general, mountains are high'. ~이/가 is not used for general facts; it points to a specific situation the speaker has just noticed or observed: 와! 산이 높다! ≈ 'this mountain I'm looking at is high!'. In comparison sentences (often joined with ~고), ~는/은 is attached to both items being compared: 이 산은 높고 저 산은 낮아요; 문법은 어렵고 단어는 쉬워요. The difference is one of nuance, not of English translation.

points.title: ~는/은 vs ~이/가: general statements and immediate experience
points.function: Choose the topic particle or the subject particle according to the nuance you want.
points.explanation: ~는/은 (는 after a vowel, 은 after a consonant) marks a noun as the topic. It is typical of general statements ('mountains are high', 'summer weather is good', 'diamonds are hard') and of comparisons ('the food here isn't good, but the weather is'). ~이/가 (가 after a vowel, 이 after a consonant) marks the subject and is typical when the speaker describes one specific thing that he is experiencing or has just noticed right now (날씨가 좋다 = the weather I am feeling right now is good). The same sentence can be correct with either particle; only the situation tells you which nuance is meant. Neither particle has an English translation.

points.title: Present Progressive: ~고 있다
points.function: Say that someone is currently in the middle of doing an action ('I am ~ing').
points.explanation: Attach ~고 있다 directly to a verb stem to show that the action is going on right now. 있다 here is a verb, which matters for the plain/diary form (~고 있다, not ~고 있는다... and it never becomes an adjective form). It can also be put into the past (~고 있었다 = 'I was ~ing') and the future (~고 있을 것이다 = 'I will be ~ing'), although in most situations a plain past or future conjugation sounds more natural. 살다 is often used as 살고 있다 for 'I live in ___', and the place can be marked with either 에서 or 에 (에서 is considered more correct). 알고 있다 must be translated as 'I know', and ~를/을 가지고 있다 as 'I have ___'.

points.title: ~아/어 있다: being in a state
points.function: Express the resulting state of an action (sitting, standing, switched on, alive) rather than the action in progress.
points.explanation: With position verbs and other state-like words, ~고 있다 describes the process, while ~아/어 있다 describes the state that results. 앉아 있다 = to be (already) seated, 서 있다 = to be standing, 누워 있다 = to be lying down. The same pattern works for state-like passive words (켜져 있다 = to be on, 꺼져 있다 = to be off, 잠겨 있다 = to be locked) and for 살다 (살아 있다 = to be alive, as opposed to 살고 있다 = to live somewhere).

points.title: 가지고 있다: to have / to possess
points.function: Say that you have (own) an object.
points.explanation: 가지다 means 'to have/possess', but to say 'I have ___' Koreans normally use ~를/을 가지고 있다 rather than plain 가지다. Even though the form looks progressive, it must be translated as 'I have ___', because English does not say 'I am having'. Note that 있다 by itself can also express having, but then the object takes ~이/가 (나는 펜이 있다) because that 있다 is an adjective. For people you 'have' (family, a girlfriend), only 있다 may be used.

points.title: 알고 있다 and 알았어 / 알겠습니다
points.function: Say that you know something, and say 'okay / got it' in reply.
points.explanation: 알고 있다 is very common in Korean and simply means 'I know' (나는 그것을 알고 있어 = 나는 그것을 알아). 알다 is also how Koreans say 'okay' when they accept a piece of information or a command: casually 알았어, politely 알았어요, and in formal situations the future-tense formal conjugation 알겠습니다 ('understood, I got it').
points.culture_note: 알겠습니다 is the standard formal acknowledgement to a superior at work or in the military; 알았어 would be rude in those situations.

drills.translation: I know that rumor.
drills.hint: the ~고 form of the verb meaning to know

drills.translation: Yes, understood.
drills.hint: formal acknowledgement built on the verb for knowing

drills.translation: Do you know the title of this song?
drills.hint: the knowing verb in its ~고 form, in a question about what someone knows now

drills.translation: Okay, got it. I'll send it by tomorrow.
drills.hint: polite past of the knowing verb, used to accept what you have just been told

drills.sentence: 저는 그때 이미 그 계획을 알고 {{answer}}.
drills.translation: I already knew about that plan at that time.
drills.hint: the standing-knowledge phrase ends with the existence verb; put that one in the polite past
drills.transliteration: jeoneun geuttae imi geu gyehoegeul algo {{answer}}.

drills.translation: I am well aware of that problem too.
drills.hint: the polite present existence verb that completes the standing-knowledge phrase

points.title: Adjective + ~아/어지다: to become (adjective)
points.function: Change an adjective from 'to be ___' into 'to get/become ___'.
points.explanation: Add ~아/어지다 to an adjective stem to create a verb meaning 'to get/become (adjective)'. The whole construction is a verb, so it follows verb conjugation rules (diary form 추워진다, not 추워지다). Because the result is a verb, principles that cannot attach to adjectives can now be used: 예뻐지고 있어요 (is getting pretty), 행복해지고 싶어 (want to become happy). The present tense is only used for general truths or repeated events; past and future tenses are far more common.

drills.translation: If you drink warm tea, your body gets warm.
drills.hint: present polite 'becomes warm'

drills.translation: Our puppy got a lot bigger last year.
drills.hint: past polite 'became big'

drills.translation: I became happy after hearing that news.
drills.hint: past polite 'became happy'

drills.translation: My skin is getting soft these days.
drills.hint: the ~고 form of 'becoming soft'

drills.translation: I want to become happy.
drills.hint: the ~고 form of 'becoming happy'

drills.translation: If you attach '-eojida' to the adjective 'haengbokhada', it becomes 'to become happy'.
drills.hint: 기본형(사전형)으로 쓰세요: 상태로 '변화한다'는 뜻의 형태

drills.translation: If you attach '-eojida' to the adjective 'chupda', it becomes 'to get cold'.
drills.hint: Dictionary (base) form of the 'become + adjective' construction meaning 'to turn cold'.

drills.translation: If you attach '-eojida' to the adjective 'chupda', it becomes 'chuwojida'.
drills.hint: Give the plain dictionary form of the 'become + adjective' construction built on 춥다 (irregular ㅂ stem).

drills.translation: If you attach '-eojida' to the adjective 'keuda', it becomes the verb 'to grow bigger'.
drills.hint: 기본형(사전형)으로 쓰세요 — '점점 크게 되다'라는 뜻의 동사.

drills.translation: If you attach '-어지다' to '어렵다', it becomes '어려워지다' (to become difficult).
drills.hint: Give the plain dictionary form of the resulting 'become + adjective' verb (ㅂ-irregular).

points.title: Tenses of ~아/어지다 (example: 추워지다)
points.function: Conjugate a 'become + adjective' verb across the tenses.
points.explanation: Because ~아/어지다 creates a verb, it takes ordinary verb conjugations: diary form 추워진다, casual present 추워져, polite present 추워져요, past 추워졌어(요), future 추워질 거예요, and progressive 추워지고 있어요.

drills.translation: The weather gets cold every night.
drills.hint: plain diary form of 'gets cold'

drills.translation: The air gets cold at dawn.
drills.hint: casual present of 'gets cold'

drills.translation: The weather gets cold every night.
drills.hint: polite present of 'gets cold'

drills.translation: The weather got cold over the weekend.
drills.hint: polite past of 'got cold'

drills.translation: From tomorrow the weather will get cold.
drills.hint: polite future of 'will get cold'

drills.translation: The weather is gradually getting cold these days.
drills.hint: polite progressive 'is getting cold'

drills.translation: University classes will get difficult next year.
drills.hint: polite future of 'become difficult'

drills.translation: The price of oil got expensive last year.
drills.hint: polite past of 'became expensive'

drills.translation: When night falls, the desert suddenly gets cold.
drills.hint: Use the adjective meaning 'cold' with the 'become' construction, in plain diary-style present tense.

drills.translation: When night falls, the weather suddenly gets cold.
drills.hint: Use 춥다 + -아/어지다 in the present informal polite (해요) form: 'becomes cold'.

drills.translation: The wind started blowing yesterday, and the weather suddenly got cold.
drills.hint: '춥다'에 '-아/어지다'를 붙여 변화를 나타내고, 과거 시제 + informal polite 어미(-어요)로 만드세요.

drills.translation: Starting next week, the weather will suddenly get cold.
drills.hint: Use the '-아/어지다' change-of-state verb for '춥다' in the future-guess form, polite informal style (해요체).

drills.translation: Now that it's October, the morning air is gradually getting colder.
drills.hint: Use the progressive (-고 있다) of the verb meaning 'to become cold', in informal polite style.

points.title: 더: 'more' in Korean sentences
points.function: Say that something is more ___ or that an action happens more.
points.explanation: 더 means 'more' and is placed before the adjective or verb it modifies: 여기는 더 편해요 (it's more comfortable here), 저는 더 공부할 거예요 (I will study more). No specific point of comparison has to be mentioned. 조금 더 means 'a little bit more'. With a verb, an adverb often follows 더 to show the degree (더 열심히 공부하다 = study harder). With counters, 더 comes right after the counted phrase (펜 두 개가 더 있어 = I have two more pens). 더 좋다 means 'better' and 더 많다 means 'there is more'.

drills.sentence: 저는 다음 학기에 {{answer}} 열심히 공부할 거예요.
drills.translation: Next semester I will study harder.
drills.hint: the word meaning 'to a greater degree'
drills.transliteration: jeoneun daeum hakgie {{answer}} yeolsimhi gongbuhal geoyeyo.

drills.translation: Three more guests came.
drills.hint: word added after a counter to mean an extra amount

drills.translation: I will wait a little bit longer.
drills.hint: goes with 조금 to mean 'a little bit ___'

drills.translation: Which one is better?
drills.hint: one syllable in front of the adjective turns 'good' into 'better'

drills.translation: More coffee, please.
drills.hint: asks for an additional amount, standing right before the request verb

drills.translation: I can't wait any longer.
drills.hint: pairs with 이상 to make the phrase 'any longer' in a negative sentence

drills.translation: There is more juice in the fridge.
drills.hint: goes before the existence verb to say an additional amount is there

points.title: 동안: 'for' a time and 'during' a noun
points.function: Express a duration ('for ten years') or a period ('during class').
points.explanation: 동안 placed after a length of time means 'for' (10년 동안 = for 10 years). Placed after an ordinary noun it means 'during' (방학 동안 = during vacation, 수업 시간 동안 = during class).

drills.translation: I studied Korean for 10 years.
drills.hint: word after a time span meaning 'for'

drills.translation: The students were quiet during class.
drills.hint: word after a noun meaning 'during'

drills.translation: How long did you live in Korea?
drills.hint: follows 얼마 to ask about a stretch of time rather than an amount

drills.translation: I am going to drive for three hours.
drills.hint: after a length of time it gives the span the action will cover

drills.translation: I worked a part-time job during vacation.
drills.hint: after an ordinary noun it marks the period something happened in

drills.translation: I didn't drink coffee for a week.
drills.hint: after a length of time; the negation belongs to the verb, not to this word

drills.translation: Please turn off your cell phone during the meeting.
drills.hint: after an event noun, it marks the stretch of time the request covers

points.title: Comparatives with ~보다 and 더
points.function: Say that something is/does more than something else.
points.explanation: Attach ~보다 directly to the noun that is the standard of comparison (X보다 = 'than X'), and put 더 ('more') before the verb or adjective. ~보다 works with verbs (나는 남동생보다 밥을 더 먹었어), with adverbs added for degree (더 열심히 공부하다 = study harder), and with counters (펜이 두 개 더 있다 = to have two more pens). The adjectives 좋다 and 많다 are extremely common in these sentences (돈이 더 많아요 = to have more money). Two nouns that ~보다 is very often attached to are 평소 (평소보다 = than usual) and 생각 (생각보다 = than I thought). Either the noun with ~보다 or 더 can be dropped; 더 alone just means 'more' without naming the standard.

drills.translation: I am taller than my older brother.
drills.hint: particle attached to the standard of comparison

drills.translation: Today is colder than yesterday.
drills.hint: one-syllable adverb meaning 'to a greater degree'

drills.translation: I am busier than usual today.
drills.hint: noun meaning 'normal/ordinary times'

drills.translation: This road is closer than I thought.
drills.hint: noun meaning 'thought, idea'

drills.translation: I have more money than long ago.
drills.hint: polite present form of the adjective meaning 'to be plentiful'

drills.translation: My younger brother eats more than I do.
drills.hint: the degree word that goes before 많이 once a ~보다 phrase has named the standard

drills.sentence: 이 식당이 저 식당{{answer}} 더 싸요?
drills.translation: Is this restaurant cheaper than that one?
drills.hint: attaches straight onto the noun that sets the standard, with no space and no other particle
drills.transliteration: i sikdangi jeo sikdang{{answer}} deo ssayo?

points.title: 덜 – Less
points.function: Say that something happens/is the case to a lesser degree.
points.explanation: 덜 is the opposite of 더 and is placed before the verb or adjective, usually together with a ~보다 phrase: 나는 남동생보다 덜 잘생겼어 (I'm less handsome than my brother). These sentences are grammatical, but Koreans usually prefer to flip the sentence and use 더 instead (남동생이 나보다 더 잘생겼어).
points.culture_note: Pronouncing 덜 as 들 is cute/funny slang; Korean speakers often enjoy hearing foreigners use it.

drills.translation: This movie is less interesting than that movie.
drills.hint: one-syllable adverb meaning 'to a smaller degree'

drills.translation: I drink less coffee these days.
drills.hint: one syllable before the verb, saying the action happens to a smaller degree

drills.translation: Does it hurt less if I take this medicine?
drills.hint: the opposite of the word for 'more', placed before the adjective in a question

drills.translation: I will be less busy next week.
drills.hint: lowers the degree of what follows; the future ending is unaffected

drills.translation: The meat is still undercooked.
drills.hint: before a verb it can mean 'not all the way'; with cooking that reads as underdone

drills.translation: Please put in less sugar.
drills.hint: reduces the amount in a request, standing directly before the verb

drills.translation: I walked less this week than last week.
drills.hint: with a ~보다 phrase naming the standard, this lowers the degree of the past verb

points.title: 낫다 – to be better
points.function: Say that one thing is better than another, or that an illness has gotten better.
points.explanation: 낫다 is very close in meaning to 좋다, but it is used naturally when a specific comparison is being made, so it appears constantly with ~보다 (라면보다 밥이 더 나아요). 낫다 is ㅅ-irregular: the ㅅ drops before a vowel, giving 나아요 / 나았어요. It is also the normal word for recovering from illness (감기가 나았어요 = my cold is better); here the comparison to the earlier sick period is understood from context, so ~보다 is not needed.

drills.translation: '좋다' and 'to be better' have similar meanings.
drills.hint: dictionary form of the comparative adjective

drills.translation: Tea is better than coffee.
drills.hint: polite present of the comparative adjective

drills.translation: That student's attitude is better than last week.
drills.hint: polite present of the comparative adjective

drills.translation: My cold is better now.
drills.hint: plain past of the adjective used for recovering

drills.translation: The illness is better.
drills.hint: plain past of the adjective used for recovering

drills.sentence: 비가 오니까 오늘은 그냥 집에 있는 게 {{answer}}.
drills.translation: Since it's raining, it's better to just stay home today.
drills.hint: Use the plain dictionary (citation) form of the adjective meaning 'to be better/preferable'.
drills.transliteration: biga onikka oneureun geunyang jibe inneun ge ___.

drills.translation: After I took the medicine, my cold got completely better.
drills.hint: Use the ㅅ-irregular verb meaning 'to get better/heal' in the past polite ~요 form.

points.title: Superlatives with 가장/제일
points.function: Say 'the most / the -est' without changing the adjective.
points.explanation: Korean superlatives need no conjugation: just add 가장 (or its spoken synonym 제일) in front of the adjective — 예쁘다 → 가장 예쁘다 (prettiest), 아름답다 → 가장 아름답다 (most beautiful). These behave like ordinary adjectives in sentences (가족은 가장 중요해요). 가장/제일 cannot be used with a plain verb unless there is also an adverb: 나는 가장 빨리 달려 (I run the fastest), 우리가 집에 제일 늦게 도착했어요. The exception is 좋아하다: 나는 수학을 가장 좋아해 = math is my favorite. For negative superlatives it is best to use a word with the opposite meaning (제일 못생기다, 제일 어렵다) rather than adding ~지 않다 or 안.

drills.translation: In our class Minsu is the tallest.
drills.hint: two-syllable superlative word, more formal of the pair

drills.translation: I dislike winter the most.
drills.hint: the spoken synonym of the superlative word

drills.translation: Math is my favorite.
drills.hint: polite present of the verb meaning 'to like'

drills.translation: My older brother arrived home the latest.
drills.hint: adverb form of 'to be late'

drills.translation: What is the most delicious food at this restaurant?
drills.hint: the superlative word of the pair that suits writing and formal speech; it stands right in front of the describing word

drills.sentence: 어제 시험이 이번 학기 시험 중에서 제일 {{answer}}.
drills.translation: Yesterday's exam was the hardest one this semester.
drills.hint: polite past of 'to be difficult' — a negative superlative is built from an opposite-meaning word, not from a negation
drills.transliteration: eoje siheomi ibeon hakgi siheom jungeseo jeil {{answer}}.

drills.sentence: 제 동생이 우리 집에서 밥을 {{answer}} 많이 먹어요.
drills.translation: My younger sibling eats the most in our family.
drills.hint: the everyday-conversation superlative word; a plain action verb cannot carry it alone, which is why an adverb follows
drills.transliteration: je dongsaengi uri jibeseo babeul {{answer}} mani meogeoyo.

points.title: 잘하다: to do something well
points.function: Say that someone is generally good at something.
points.explanation: Use the pattern (person)는 (noun)을/를 잘하다. With 하다 verbs you simply remove 하다 to get the noun (수영하다 → 수영, 공부하다 → 공부): 나는 수영을 잘해 = I am good at swimming. 잘하다 states that your ability in general is good. It combines freely with comparatives and superlatives: 저는 수영을 작년보다 더 잘해요, 우리 아들은 축구를 가장 잘해요.

drills.translation: My friend sings well.
drills.hint: polite present of the verb for 'to be good at'

drills.translation: I am good at swimming.
drills.hint: object particle after a consonant-final noun

drills.sentence: 그 교수는 다른 교수들보다 수업을 더 {{answer}}.
drills.translation: That professor teaches classes better than the other professors.
drills.hint: polite present of the verb for 'to be good at'
drills.transliteration: geu gyosuneun dareun gyosudeulboda sueobeul deo {{answer}}.

drills.translation: My older brother does really well in school.
drills.hint: drop 하다 from the verb meaning 'to study' and use the noun that is left

drills.translation: Sumi, which sport are you good at?
drills.hint: the 'good at' verb in the polite present — a question in this style takes the same shape as a statement

drills.translation: You did really well on the presentation yesterday.
drills.hint: the 'good at' verb in the polite past, said as praise for something already finished

drills.translation: My younger sibling is good at math, and I am good at English.
drills.hint: the 'good at' verb carrying the 'and' ending that links it to the second clause

points.title: 잘: well (adverb)
points.function: Say that an action is done well in a particular situation.
points.explanation: 잘 is an adverb (removing 하다 from 잘하다 does not leave a noun) and is placed before the verb: 나는 어젯밤에 잘 잤어 (I slept well last night). The difference from 잘하다 is subtle: 나는 공부를 잘한다 says your ability in general is good, while 나는 잘 공부한다 says you are doing it well because of the current situation. Note also fixed expressions: 잘 + 생기다 → 잘생기다 (handsome), and 저는 잘 모르겠어요 = 'I don't know', where 모르겠다 (future-looking form) is used even about the present.

drills.translation: I slept well last night.
drills.hint: one-syllable adverb meaning 'in a good manner'

drills.translation: That owner treats the customers well.
drills.hint: polite present of the verb 'to treat someone'

drills.translation: I don't really know that person's name.
drills.hint: the common ~겠 form of the verb 'to not know'

drills.translation: That actor is tall and really handsome.
drills.hint: the fixed adjective for good looks, built on the 'in a good manner' adverb; its past-shaped ending describes how someone is now

drills.translation: Can you hear my voice okay?
drills.hint: the one-syllable adverb saying the action comes off nicely; it sits directly before the verb

drills.translation: I ate really well at that restaurant yesterday.
drills.hint: polite past of 'to eat' — the adverb in front already supplies the 'in a good manner' part

drills.translation: Are you doing well these days?
drills.hint: polite present of the verb for getting on and spending one's days — the standard way to ask how someone is

points.title: 못하다: to do something poorly
points.function: Say that someone is generally bad at something.
points.explanation: 못하다 is the opposite of 잘하다 and is used the same way: (noun)을/를 못하다 (나는 수영을 못해 = I am bad at swimming). Because it describes general ability, it only makes sense with skills — you would not say 밥을 못하다 to mean you can't eat right now; for a situational inability use the adverb 못. It also combines with superlatives: 저는 축구를 제일 못해요 = I play soccer the worst.

drills.translation: I am bad at swimming.
drills.hint: polite present of the verb for 'to be bad at'

drills.translation: I play soccer the worst.
drills.hint: polite present of the verb for 'to be bad at'

drills.translation: I am not very good at cooking.
drills.hint: object marker on a noun with no final consonant — the skill is the object of the ability verb

drills.translation: When I was little I was really bad at singing.
drills.hint: the 'bad at' verb in the polite past — the ability is described for a time that is over

drills.translation: I am bad with computers, so I often ask my son.
drills.hint: the 'bad at' verb carrying the 'because' ending that ties it to the result clause

drills.translation: My younger sibling is worse at English than I am.
drills.hint: the 'bad at' verb in the polite present; the comparison in front of it does not change its shape

drills.translation: I am bad at sports, but I walk every day.
drills.hint: the 'bad at' verb carrying the 'but' ending that sets up a contrast with the next clause

points.title: 못: poorly / couldn't
points.function: Say that an action was done poorly or could not be done because something prevented it.
points.explanation: The adverb 못 goes directly before the verb and has two possible meanings: (1) one does the action not well because of some situation, or (2) one did not do the action because something prevented him/her. 저는 어제 못 잤어요 can mean 'I didn't sleep well' or 'I couldn't sleep'. To force the 'not well' reading, add 잘 before 못: 저는 어제 시험을 잘 못 봤어요 = I did poorly on the exam. Otherwise the verb itself (학교에 못 갔어요 — you can't 'go somewhere well') or the situation makes the meaning clear. This contrasts with 안 / ~지 않다, which carry no sense of being prevented.

drills.translation: No, I couldn't hear (you).
drills.hint: one-syllable adverb of prevented ability

drills.translation: I did poorly on the exam yesterday.
drills.hint: adverb meaning 'in a good manner', added to remove ambiguity

drills.translation: The ticket is so expensive that I can't go to Canada.
drills.hint: one-syllable adverb of prevented ability

drills.translation: I had no time yesterday, so I could not work out.
drills.hint: the one-syllable adverb of being prevented; with a 하다 verb it slips in right before the doing part, never in front of the noun

drills.translation: I hurt my leg, so I could not go to school yesterday.
drills.hint: polite past of 'to go' — the adverb in front already carries the inability

drills.sentence: 요즘 너무 바빠서 친구를 자주 못 {{answer}}.
drills.translation: I am so busy these days that I cannot see my friends often.
drills.hint: polite present of 'to meet' — the adverb before it supplies the inability
drills.transliteration: yojeum neomu bappaseo chingureul jaju mot {{answer}}.

points.title: ~지 못하다
points.function: A longer form with the same meaning as 못 + verb.
points.explanation: Just as ~지 않다 mirrors 안, you can attach ~지 못하다 to a verb stem instead of putting 못 in front: 저는 어제 못 잤어요 = 저는 어제 자지 못했어요. Both mean 'I didn't sleep (well) / couldn't sleep last night'. Note that this is subtly different from (noun)을/를 못하다, which describes general ability: 저는 공부를 못해요 = I am bad at studying, while 저는 어제 공부하지 못했어요 = I couldn't study yesterday.

drills.translation: I couldn't sleep yesterday.
drills.hint: polite past of the auxiliary attached after ~지

drills.translation: I couldn't study yesterday.
drills.hint: the one-syllable connector before the negative auxiliary

drills.translation: I have a lot of work these days, so I cannot exercise.
drills.hint: the auxiliary that follows ~지, in the polite present

drills.translation: My grandmother's health has not been good lately.
drills.hint: 'to be good' plus the one-syllable ending that hands the clause over to the negative auxiliary; with a describing word the pattern means 'falls short'

drills.translation: Have you still not managed to get a ticket?
drills.hint: the auxiliary that follows ~지, polite past, asked as a question

drills.sentence: 아침을 먹지 {{answer}} 지금 배가 너무 고파요.
drills.translation: I could not eat breakfast, so I am really hungry now.
drills.hint: the auxiliary after ~지 carrying the 'because' ending that ties it to the next clause
drills.transliteration: achimeul meokji {{answer}} jigeum baega neomu gopayo.

drills.translation: I could not watch the movie to the end, so I just left.
drills.hint: the auxiliary after ~지 with the 'and then' ending that lets the sentence run on

points.title: 잘못 vs 잘 못
points.function: Distinguish the noun 'mistake' from the adverb phrase 'not well'.
points.explanation: Written with no space, 잘못 is a noun meaning 'mistake, fault': 그것은 제 잘못이었어요 = That was my fault. Written with a space, 잘 못 is the adverb 잘 plus 못 and means 'not well'. Note also that a few nouns prefer 제/내 over 저의/나의; 잘못 is one of them, as is 제/내 생각 ('my thought/opinion').

drills.translation: That was my fault.
drills.hint: noun meaning 'fault, error' (no space)

drills.translation: I didn't write the answer well.
drills.hint: adverb meaning 'in a good manner'

drills.translation: Whose fault is this?
drills.hint: the noun for an error or blame, written solid with nothing between its two syllables

drills.translation: My younger sibling doesn't sing well.
drills.hint: two separate words with a space between them: the adverb of good manner, then the negative that says the action does not come off

drills.translation: I'm sorry, I did something wrong.
drills.hint: the same noun for an error, here written straight onto 하다 so that it works as a verb

drills.translation: Admitting your mistakes is hard.

points.title: Asking yes/no questions with intonation
points.function: Turn any statement into a question without changing its structure.
points.explanation: When no question word (누구/무엇/언제/어디/왜/어떻게/얼마나) is involved, Korean questions need no structural change at all — simply raise the intonation at the end of the sentence: 엄마는 먹었어요 (Mom ate) → 엄마는 먹었어요? (Did mom eat?). This works in every tense. Since Korean rarely uses the word 'you', the subject is normally omitted when you are asking about the listener: 밥을 먹었어? / 집에 갔어? If the subject is someone else, state it as usual: 남동생은 울었어요?

points.title: Formal questions ~ㅂ/습니까?
points.function: Ask a question in the formal high-respect speech level.
points.explanation: The formal high-respect ending ~습니다 is never used for questions. Instead use ~ㅂ/습니까?: ~ㅂ니까 is added directly to stems ending in a vowel (가다 → 갑니까?), and ~습니까 after stems ending in a consonant (먹다 → 먹습니까?). Because past-tense stems end in ~았/었 (a consonant), the past is always ~았/었습니까? (갔습니까?). Future forms use 갈 겁니까? or 갈 것입니까?. ~ㅂ/습니까 is the most formal way to make a question and is typical of announcements, checklists and the military/business register.
points.culture_note: Public checklists (for example the daily bathroom-cleaning charts posted in Korean schools) are written almost entirely with ~ㅂ/습니까?, e.g. asking whether the floor is clean, the mirror wiped, the soap refilled.

points.title: Korean Questions ~니
points.function: Ask an informal question by ending the sentence with ~니 instead of ~아/어.
points.explanation: Attach ~니 directly to the stem of a verb, adjective or 이다. It works in every tense: past (했니, 먹었니, 갔니, 이었니), present (하니, 먹니, 가니, 이니), future with ~겠 (하겠니, 먹겠니, 가겠니) and future with ~ㄹ 것이다 (할 거니, 할 것이니, 먹을 거니, 먹을 것이니). There is no vowel choice (no ~아/어 decision): ~니 always starts with ㄴ, so it is a 'solid ㄴ' addition. The only irregular that applies is the ㄹ irregular: the ㄹ of the stem drops (열다 + ~니 = 여니, 만들다 → 만드니, 살다 → 사니).
points.culture_note: This ending has a slightly feminine feel. It is very commonly heard from female teachers in Korean schools asking students questions.

points.title: Solid ㄴ additions and the ㄹ irregular
points.function: Know which grammatical endings begin with a fixed ㄴ and therefore make a ㄹ-final stem drop its ㄹ.
points.explanation: Some additions require the speaker to choose between two options (for example ~아 vs ~어). Others have only one shape, beginning with ㄴ — these are 'solid ㄴ' additions: ~니, ~나, ~는, ~는데, ~네. Whenever a solid ㄴ addition is attached to a stem ending in ㄹ, the ㄹ is dropped and the ending is attached to what remains: 열다 → 여니, 팔다 → 파나요, 살다 → 사니.

points.title: Korean Questions ~ㄴ/은가(요)
points.function: Ask a softer question about a present state, mostly with adjectives and 이다.
points.explanation: Attach ~ㄴ/은 to an adjective stem exactly as you would when describing a noun (예쁘다 → 예쁜, 작다 → 작은), then add 가(요): 예쁜가(요)?, 작은가(요)?. With 이다 it becomes ~인가(요) and with 아니다 it becomes 아닌가(요). Adding 요 makes it more formal, but the form is still less formal than the high-respect ~ㅂ/습니까. It is only conjugated into the present tense, so it asks about a present situation. The nuance is softer, like 'would it be okay if I went into the park?' compared with 'can I go into the park?'. 아닌가(요)? is very commonly tacked onto the end of a statement to mean 'no?/isn't it?' when you doubt yourself.

points.title: Korean Questions ~나(요)
points.function: Ask a softer question with verbs, 있다 and 없다.
points.explanation: ~나(요) has the same softening function as ~ㄴ/은가(요), but it is more often used with verbs and with 있다/없다. Attach it straight to the stem: 있나?, 하나요?, 타고 있나요?. Being a solid ㄴ addition, it triggers the ㄹ irregular (팔다 → 파나요). It can be used in the past tense (있었나요?, 들었나요?, 샀나요?, 했나요?). In the future it only sounds natural with the ~겠다 conjugation; ~나(요) is normally not added to 이다, and therefore not to ~ㄹ/을 것이다 either (내일 퇴원할 거나요? / 내일 퇴원할 것이나요? are unnatural).

points.title: Why (왜)
points.function: Ask 'why' by inserting the adverb 왜 into a statement.
points.explanation: 왜 is an adverb, so it can be placed freely in the sentence, but the most common position is right before the verb. If the sentence contains other adverbs (including the negative 안), 왜 usually comes first. You can turn almost any statement into a 'why' question just by inserting 왜. 왜 is also the standard reply when someone calls your name, where English says 'what?'.
points.culture_note: Answering 왜? when someone calls your name is normal in Korean, even though translating it as 'why?' sounds strange in English.

To ask where another person or an object is, it is more natural to use 있다: 펜이 어디에 있어요?

points.title: 어때? – asking for an opinion
points.function: Ask 'how is/was …?' or 'what do you think about …?'

It sounds most natural when the thing you are asking about carries no particle (점심 어때?). ~요 makes it more formal (어때요?) and it can be put into the past tense (어땠어요?), though asking about the past does not strictly require the past tense. It sometimes corresponds to 'how about…?', but often the right English is 'how is…?/what do you think about…?'.
points.culture_note: Korean learners of English very often mistranslate 어때 as 'how about', which is only sometimes correct — 남자 친구 어때? means 'How is your boyfriend?', not 'How about your boyfriend?'.

Before 이다, 뭐 is much more common than 무엇: 이것은 뭐야?, 이름이 뭐예요? (not 이것이 무엇이야?).

points.title: What (무슨) before a noun
points.function: Ask 'what + noun' when you have no idea what the answer might be.
points.explanation: 무슨 is placed before a noun to describe it, in the same slot as an adjective (그 영화 / 무서운 영화 / 무슨 영화). Its dictionary form really is 무슨 — despite looking like an adjective with ~ㄴ/은 attached, it is not an adjective. 무슨 is used when the speaker does not know what the object is and the possible answers are essentially unlimited: 무슨 냄새야?, 무슨 소리야?, 무슨 생각(을) 해?, 무슨 말이야? (the last two often mean 'what do you mean?').

drills.translation: What are you thinking about?
drills.hint: 'what' word placed before a noun

drills.translation: What skirt did you buy at that store?
drills.hint: 'what' word placed before a noun

drills.translation: What is this sound?
drills.hint: 'what' word placed before a noun

drills.translation: What day of the week is it today?
drills.hint: the 'what' word that fills the adjective slot before a noun; the fixed way to ask about the day

drills.translation: What food are you going to make this weekend?
drills.hint: the 'what' word before a noun, with a future-tense verb; the possible answers are wide open

drills.translation: What problem do you have?
drills.hint: the 'what' word describing a noun that is the subject of the sentence

points.title: Which (어떤 / 어느)
points.function: Ask 'which + noun', choosing from options or asking about characteristics.
points.explanation: 어떤 and 어느 are placed before nouns to describe them, just like 무슨, but they usually translate as 'which': 어떤 영화를 보고 싶어요? = Which movie do you want to see? 어떤 is used (1) to choose from a limited selection of options, and (2) to ask about the type, properties or characteristics of a person/object (van, SUV, truck…). 무슨 by contrast is used when the answer could be anything, so 어떤 usually should not replace 무슨 in sentences like 무슨 냄새야? The difference between them is subtle and swapping them often gives essentially the same meaning. 어떤 also carries the meaning 'some/a certain'.

drills.translation: Which lotion do you want to use?
drills.hint: 'which' word used when choosing from options or asking about type

drills.translation: Which one is better?
drills.hint: 'which' word placed before a noun

drills.translation: Which car do you want to buy?
drills.hint: 'which' word asking about type or selection

drills.translation: Which country are you from?
drills.hint: 'which' word for singling one out of a known, closed set such as countries

drills.translation: Which way do I have to go?
drills.hint: 'which' word for choosing between a small number of options already in front of you

drills.translation: What kind of music do you like?
drills.hint: 'which' word used to ask about the type or characteristics of something, not to pick off a fixed list

points.title: 무슨, 어떤 and 어느: asking 'what' and 'which' before nouns
points.function: Choose the right determiner when asking 'what ___?' or 'which ___?' about a noun.
points.explanation: All three words are placed immediately before a noun. 무슨 is used when the speaker has no idea at all what the answer might be (the answer usually identifies the source or identity of something). 어떤 is used to ask about the type or characteristics of something, and also when the listener has a set of options to choose from. 어느 is used only for choosing among options; it cannot ask about characteristics and cannot refer to something completely unknown. Because the usages overlap, the three are often interchangeable in practice, so it is just as important to learn where each one must NOT be used.
