drills.hint: determiner used when you cannot guess the answer at all

drills.translation: What song are you listening to right now?
drills.hint: determiner for a completely unpredictable answer

drills.hint: determiner asking about type or qualities

drills.translation: What kind of smell does this flower have?
drills.hint: determiner asking for a description of qualities

drills.hint: determiner used when options are given

drills.translation: Which university do you want to go to?
drills.hint: determiner for picking from a selection

drills.hint: determiner used only when choosing from options

drills.translation: Which car shall we buy?
drills.hint: determiner meaning 'which one of these'

drills.translation: What is that smell? I can't see anything.

points.title: 어떤 to mean 'some / a certain'
points.function: Refer to a noun the speaker is aware of but cannot specify.
points.explanation: Apart from questions, 어떤 placed before a noun means 'some (unspecified)'. The speaker knows that a person/thing was involved but does not know or does not state exactly which one. 무슨 and 어느 cannot be used this way.

drills.hint: determiner meaning 'some/a certain (unidentified)'

drills.translation: I read some book at the library yesterday.
drills.hint: determiner used when the speaker can't specify which one

drills.translation: My friend went into some building.
drills.hint: determiner for an unspecified noun

drills.translation: Some people don't drink milk.
drills.hint: determiner meaning 'some' before a plural noun — a subset the speaker does not identify

drills.translation: He quit the company for some reason.
drills.hint: determiner meaning 'a certain' — the speaker will not say what the reason was

drills.translation: Some child is crying outside right now.
drills.hint: determiner for an unidentified person — the speaker can hear the child but does not know who it is

points.title: 몇 + counter: asking 'how many'
points.function: Ask how many of something there are, what time it is, or how old someone is.
points.explanation: To ask 'how many ___?' put 몇 directly before the appropriate counter: 몇 대, 몇 명, 몇 번, 몇 개, 몇 살, 몇 시. The noun being counted usually keeps its particle (차가 몇 대 있어요?), and no particle is attached to 몇 + counter, because 몇 + counter functions as a question word. Attaching a particle after the counter (차 몇 대가 있어요?) is still understandable but less natural. Note that the exact same word order without question intonation means 'some / a few' as a statement.

drills.translation: How many computers did that company buy?
drills.hint: question word for counting machines

drills.translation: How many friends did you meet?
drills.hint: question word for counting people

drills.translation: How many students are in the classroom?
drills.hint: question word for counting persons

drills.translation: How many times did you go to school yesterday?
drills.hint: question word for counting occurrences

drills.translation: How many times did you rip that paper?
drills.hint: question word asking about repetitions

drills.translation: How many files did you send?
drills.hint: question word for counting items

drills.translation: How many pieces of bread did you eat?
drills.hint: question word for counting separate objects

drills.translation: How old is your younger brother?
drills.hint: question word for years of age (casual ending)

drills.translation: How old are you?
drills.hint: question word for asking someone's age

drills.translation: What time is it now?
drills.hint: question word for the hour on the clock

points.title: 얼마나: asking 'how (much)'
points.function: Ask to what extent something is or happens, or how much of something uncountable.
points.explanation: 얼마나 goes before adjectives and adverbs to mean 'how ___' (얼마나 짧다 = how short, 얼마나 자주 = how often, 얼마나 빨리 = how quickly, 얼마나 잘 = how well). Before verbs it means 'how much', used when the speaker is not distinguishing countable objects but asking about an uncountable amount. 많이 can be inserted (얼마나 많이 먹었어요?) with the same translation; it stresses that the speaker already assumes the answer is 'a lot'. 많다 can also be used as a modifier (얼마나 많은 빵을 먹었어요?), which is correct but sounds much less natural. If you ARE distinguishing countable objects, use 몇 + counter instead. 얼마나 is different from 어떻게, which asks about method.

references.title: Unit 1, Lesson 22 – How many, How much (얼마나)

drills.hint: adverb meaning 'to what extent' before another adverb

drills.translation: How much water did you drink yesterday?
drills.hint: adverb asking about an uncountable amount

drills.translation: How much space does that desk take up?
drills.hint: adverb asking 'how much' with a verb

drills.hint: the 'how much' adverb, here measuring a length of time

drills.translation: How tall is that person?
drills.hint: the 'how ___' adverb placed directly before an adjective

points.title: 얼마: asking how much something costs
points.function: Ask the price or amount of something.
points.explanation: 얼마 is a noun meaning 'how much (money/amount)' and is normally used with 이다: 얼마예요?, 얼마였어요?. Although related in meaning, 얼마 and 얼마나 are technically different words. Remember that 이게, 그게 and 저게 are contractions of 이것이, 그것이 and 저것이.

drills.hint: noun asking about price (polite ~예요 ending)

drills.translation: How much was the fine?
drills.hint: noun for amount, in the past tense of 이다

drills.translation: How much is this umbrella?
drills.hint: noun asking a price, with the casual (반말) copula ending

drills.translation: How much is this bag?
drills.hint: noun asking a price, with the formal ~입니까 ending

drills.translation: How much did you buy those shoes for?

points.title: Using question words on their own
points.function: React to what someone said with a one-word question asking for more information.
points.explanation: 누구, 뭐, 언제, 어디, 왜 and 어떻게 can each stand alone as a complete question asking for the missing information about what was just said. 요 can be added to any of them in more formal situations. Use 누가 (not 누구) when you are asking about the acting subject, and 누구(를) / 뭐(를) when asking about the object. 왜? is also the standard reply when someone calls your name ('what do you want?').

drills.hint: one-word question asking for a reason

drills.hint: one-word question about time

drills.hint: one-word question about place

drills.hint: one-word question about the person receiving the action

drills.translation: I'm going to the airport. – How?
drills.hint: one-word question about the method

drills.translation: My friend bought something strange yesterday. – What?
drills.hint: one-word question about the thing itself

points.title: ~는/은 and ~이/가 revisited: nuance and form
points.function: Choose between the topic particle and the subject particle according to nuance.
points.explanation: Form: ~는 and ~가 attach after a vowel, ~은 and ~이 after a consonant. Usage of ~는/은: (1) to simply mark the subject, (2) to compare something (이 산은 높다 – but maybe another is low), (3) to state a general fact (다이아몬드는 딱딱하다). Usage of ~이/가: (1) to mark the subject, (2) to point out something based on a recent experience/observation (날씨가 좋다! 비가 와요!), (3) to stress that it is that particular subject who does the action or has the quality — typically in the answer to a 누가 question (누가 그녀를 좋아해? – 내가 그녀를 좋아해), (4) on the 'object' of sentences predicated by adjectives (나는 학교가 싫다, 나는 펜이 있다), (5) on the noun before 아니다 (나는 학생이 아니다), (6) on the noun before 되다 (나는 의사가 되고 싶다). It is also used on the noun in state-passive sentences (문이 열려 있다), since a particular door in a particular situation is being described. All of this is situational: 내 친구가 밥을 먹었다 and 내 친구는 밥을 먹었다 can be identical depending on context — 'it's not about understanding them, it's about understanding when to use them.'

drills.hint: topic particle used after a vowel

drills.translation: Bananas are yellow.
drills.hint: topic particle stating a general fact after a vowel

drills.translation: This mountain is high (another one may be low).
drills.hint: topic particle used after a consonant, here for comparison

drills.translation: Summer weather is nice.
drills.hint: topic particle in a general statement (word ends in a vowel sound? no — consonant-final noun)

drills.translation: The cat is behind the house.
drills.hint: subject particle after a vowel

drills.translation: The weather is nice!
drills.hint: subject particle marking a fresh observation

drills.translation: The door is open.
drills.hint: subject particle after a consonant, in a state sentence

drills.translation: I have a pen.
drills.hint: subject particle on the noun before 있다

drills.hint: particle that stresses the subject in an answer to a 'who' question

drills.sentence: 너는 누구를 좋아해? – 나{{answer}} 그녀를 좋아해.

drills.hint: plain subject marker used when the stress is on the object
drills.transliteration: neoneun nugureul joahae? – na{{answer}} geunyeoreul joahae.

drills.translation: I want to become a doctor.
drills.hint: particle required on the noun before 되다

drills.translation: I am not a student.

points.title: ~기 전에 (before doing)
points.function: Say 'before [verb]-ing' by attaching ~기 전에 to a verb stem.
points.explanation: Attach ~기 전에 directly to the plain verb stem (오다 → 오기 전에, 먹다 → 먹기 전에). The clause before ~기 전에 is never conjugated for tense — the tense of the whole sentence is shown only by the verb of the main clause (엄마가 오기 전에 나는 먹었어 / 먹을 거야). The subject of the ~기 전에 clause almost always takes ~이/가. The one exception is when both clauses share the same subject: then you may put ~는/은 on that subject once in the first clause and drop it from the second (나는 오기 전에 밥을 먹었어). Using ~는/은 instead of ~이/가 on the sub-clause subject can add a contrastive feeling ('I was the person who…'). The whole ~기 전에 clause functions as a single time expression, like 어제, so it can also be placed later in the sentence, not only at the front.

drills.hint: prior to someone's arrival

drills.translation: My younger sibling lived in China before coming to Korea.
drills.hint: before arriving here

drills.hint: prior to having a meal

drills.translation: I got water ready before taking the medicine.
drills.hint: before swallowing it

drills.translation: I looked out the window before putting on my coat.
drills.hint: before putting the clothing on

drills.translation: I closed the window before leaving the house.
drills.hint: before stepping outside

drills.translation: My older sister worked in Busan before she got married.
drills.hint: before the wedding took place

drills.translation: Before mom came, I ate.
drills.hint: 'before ___ arrives' clause built on 오다

drills.translation: My younger brother drank milk before going to school.
drills.hint: 'before going' clause built on 가다

drills.translation: Before mom comes, I will eat.
drills.hint: future/intention form of 'to eat', casual style — the tense goes here, not in the first clause

drills.translation: It's good to wash newly bought clothes once before putting them on.
drills.hint: Use the 'before doing X' pattern (verb stem + 기 전에) with the verb meaning 'to wear/put on'.

drills.translation: Before going out of the house, please be sure to close the windows.
drills.hint: Use the verb meaning 'to go out' with the '-기 전에' pattern ('before doing').

points.title: ~ㄴ/은 후에 (after doing)
points.function: Say 'after [verb]-ing' by attaching ~ㄴ/은 후에 to a verb stem.
points.explanation: Unlike ~기 전에, you do NOT add ~기 before 후. Add ~은 to a stem ending in a consonant (먹다 → 먹은 후에) and ~ㄴ directly to a stem ending in a vowel (가다 → 간 후에, 끝나다 → 끝난 후에). The resulting clause behaves like ~기 전에: it is one time-expression unit and the tense of the sentence is shown by the main clause. Korean speakers also use ~ㄴ/은 후에 where English would say 'since'.

points.title: Time expression + 후에 (later / from now)
points.function: Say how far in the future something will happen: 'in ___ / ___ from now'.
points.explanation: Place 후에 after an amount of time (seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, years) to mean 'later / from now'. These units are used intuitively just like expressions with 전. Note that hours are counted with native Korean numbers, and the writer's habit is to spell the number out (열 시간 후에) rather than use a numeral.

points.title: ~ㄴ/은 다음에 (after doing) — 다음 for 후
points.function: An alternative to ~ㄴ/은 후에 with exactly the same meaning.
points.explanation: You can substitute 다음 for 후 in the ~ㄴ/은 후에 construction: 먹은 다음에, 끝난 다음에, 신은 다음에, 치운 다음에. The rule for ~ㄴ vs ~은 is identical (consonant-final stem → ~은, vowel-final stem → ~ㄴ), and the meaning does not change.

drills.translation: After I ate, I met a friend.
drills.hint: 'after eating', using the word for 'next' instead of 후

drills.translation: What are you going to eat after you exercise?
drills.hint: 'after exercising' — build it on 하다 and use the word for 'next' where 후 would go

drills.translation: After you brush your teeth, don't eat anything.
drills.hint: 'after brushing' — from 닦다, a consonant-final stem, with 'next' in place of 후

drills.translation: After we watched the movie, we drank coffee.
drills.hint: 'after watching' — from 보다, a vowel-final stem, with 'next' in place of 후

drills.translation: I always eat after washing my hands.
drills.hint: 'after washing' — from 씻다, consonant-final, using 'next' rather than 후

drills.translation: After all my friends had left, I started cleaning.
drills.hint: 'after they left' — from 가다, vowel-final, using 'next' rather than 후

points.title: 직전에 / 직후에 (right before / right after)
points.function: Stress that something happened immediately before or immediately after something else.
points.explanation: 직전 and 직후 are used exactly like 전 and 후 (verb stem + ~기 직전에; verb stem + ~ㄴ/은 직후에; time expression + 직전에/직후에). The added 직 emphasizes that the action came immediately before or immediately after the other action or point in time.

drills.translation: Right before having dinner, my son ate snacks.
drills.hint: immediately before the meal happened

drills.translation: Right after I put on the suit, I went outside.
drills.hint: immediately after getting dressed

drills.translation: Right before the exam, my stomach hurt.
drills.hint: goes straight onto a time noun: the moment immediately before it

drills.translation: I got a job right after graduating.
drills.hint: goes straight onto a noun such as 'graduation': the moment immediately following it

drills.translation: I barely got on the bus right before it left.
drills.hint: 출발하다, turned into 'the instant before it leaves'

drills.translation: Right after I got off the subway, I realised my wallet was gone.
drills.hint: 내리다, turned into 'the instant after getting off'

points.title: ~ㄴ/은 이래로 (since)
points.function: Express 'since (doing something)' in a formal, literary way.
points.explanation: 이래로 can replace 후 in ~ㄴ/은 후에 to mean 'since I…': 한국에 온 이래로, 열심히 공부한 이래로. These sentences are perfectly correct, but Korean people rarely say 이래로; the natural choice is ~ㄴ/은 후에 even where English says 'since'.

drills.translation: Since coming to Korea, I have been learning Korean.
drills.hint: formal 'since arriving' form of 오다

drills.translation: Since studying hard, my skills have improved quickly.
drills.hint: formal 'since studying' form

drills.translation: Since receiving the scholarship, I have been studying harder.
drills.hint: the bookish 'since receiving' form of 받다 — a consonant-final stem

drills.sentence: 그 사고가 {{answer}} 저는 밤에 운전을 안 해요.
drills.translation: Since that accident happened, I don't drive at night.
drills.hint: the bookish 'since it happened' form of 나다 — a vowel-final stem
drills.transliteration: geu sagoga {{answer}} jeoneun bame unjeoneul an haeyo.

drills.sentence: 그 책을 {{answer}} 세상을 보는 눈이 달라졌어요.
drills.translation: Since reading that book, the way I see the world has changed.
drills.hint: the literary 'since reading' form of 읽다, the kind of wording you meet in print
drills.transliteration: geu chaegeul {{answer}} sesangeul boneun nuni dallajyeosseoyo.

drills.sentence: 선생님을 처음 {{answer}} 벌써 십 년이 지났어요.
drills.translation: Ten years have already passed since I first met my teacher.
drills.hint: the literary 'since meeting' form of 만나다
drills.transliteration: seonsaengnimeul cheoeum {{answer}} beolsseo sip nyeoni jinasseoyo.

drills.translation: Have you ever regretted it since you quit the company?
drills.hint: the bookish 'since quitting' form of 그만두다, here inside a question

points.title: 안 / 이내 (within a period of time)
points.function: Say that something will happen within a certain amount of time.
points.explanation: 안 normally means 'inside' (집 안에 = inside the house). When 안 or 이내 follows an indication of time, it means 'within' that period: 5년 안에 / 5년 이내에, 1년 안에 / 1년 이내. The two are interchangeable in meaning; ~에 is usually attached (이내 can also appear without it).

drills.sentence: 나는 5년 {{answer}} 외국어 다섯 개를 배우고 싶어.
drills.translation: I want to learn five foreign languages within five years.
drills.hint: the everyday word for 'inside', used here as 'within'
drills.transliteration: naneun o-nyeon ___ oegugeo daseot gaereul baeugo sipeo.

drills.translation: We will get married within one year.
drills.hint: the more formal word for 'within'

drills.sentence: 이 일을 한 시간 {{answer}} 끝낼 수 있어요?
drills.translation: Can you finish this work within an hour?
drills.hint: sets the one-hour limit: the plain noun meaning 'inside a place', carrying 에
drills.transliteration: i ireul han sigan {{answer}} kkeunnael su isseoyo?

drills.sentence: 숙제를 오늘 {{answer}} 다 못 할 것 같아요.
drills.translation: I don't think I can finish all the homework before the day is out.
drills.hint: casual speech, with today as the deadline — the ordinary 'inside' word plus 에
drills.transliteration: sukjereul oneul {{answer}} da mot hal geot gatayo.

drills.translation: You have to apply for a refund within 14 days of receiving the item.
drills.hint: shop-policy wording: the formal 'within', with 에 on it

drills.translation: We'll let you know the interview result within a week.
drills.hint: polite business register: the stiffer word for 'within', still carrying 에

drills.translation: This item is delivered within three days.
drills.hint: the formal 'within' left bare, no particle, right in front of the noun

points.title: 모든 + noun (every / all ___)
points.function: Say 'every ___' or 'all ___' before a noun.
points.explanation: 모든 is placed directly before a noun: 모든 것 (everything), 모든 사람 (all people), 모든 과일, 모든 선생님. It looks and behaves like an adjective in the ~ㄴ describing form (like 예쁜, 아름다운, 똑똑한), but there is no dictionary form 모드다 and it can never predicate a clause — you cannot end a sentence with 모든. Compared with 다, 모든 says the action applies to every one of the nouns individually, while 다 says one action was carried out to completion leaving nothing behind.

drills.translation: All Asian people use chopsticks well.
drills.hint: the determiner meaning 'every', placed before a noun

drills.translation: All the students slept all day long.
drills.hint: the determiner meaning 'every', placed before a noun

drills.translation: Does every customer have to make a reservation?
drills.hint: the one-word 'every' that sits in front of a noun; here it opens a question

drills.translation: Not everything in this shop is cheap.
drills.hint: the 'every' word before the noun — the ending of the sentence does the denying

drills.translation: That company sells everything online.
drills.hint: the 'every' determiner, here in front of the word for 'thing'

drills.translation: The teacher kindly answered every question.
drills.hint: the 'every' word placed before the noun; it never takes an ending of its own

drills.sentence: 이 도서관에서는 {{answer}} 책을 무료로 빌릴 수 있어요.
drills.translation: At this library you can borrow any book free of charge.
drills.hint: the determiner meaning 'all', which looks like a ~ㄴ describing form but comes from no verb
drills.transliteration: i doseogwaneseoneun {{answer}} chaegeul muryoro billil su isseoyo.

points.title: 다 (all — adverb of completion)
points.function: Say that an action was done completely / that all members of a group do something.
points.explanation: 다 is an adverb. (1) With an object it shows the action was finished with nothing left behind: 저는 숙제를 다 했어요. (2) With a plural/group subject it shows all of its members do the action or have the quality: 사람들이 다 왔어요, 남자들은 다 게을러요. It works in negative sentences too (사람들이 다 안 왔어요 = not all the people came). No object particle is ever attached to 다. 다 can also be used as a noun before 이다/아니다: 그게 다야? / 이게 다가 아니야. 다 may co-occur with 모든 or 모두 in the same sentence.

drills.translation: I did all of my homework.
drills.hint: one-syllable adverb meaning 'entirely, with nothing left'

drills.translation: All the people have come.
drills.hint: one-syllable adverb meaning 'every one of them'

drills.translation: Is that all?
drills.hint: the noun 'all' plus the casual 이다 ending

drills.translation: Did you drink all the milk?
drills.hint: adverb of completion, here in a question — the carton was left empty; it never takes an object particle

drills.translation: The students in my class are all kind.
drills.hint: one-syllable adverb saying every member of the group shares the quality

drills.translation: Don't spend all the money.
drills.hint: adverb of completion in a negative command — spend it down to nothing

points.title: 모두 (all / everybody, everything)
points.function: Say 'all' as an adverb or 'everybody/everything' as a pronoun.
points.explanation: As an adverb 모두 means the same as 다 (선생님들은 모두 똑똑해요 = 선생님들은 다 똑똑해요), and 다 may even follow it (모두 다 똑똑해요). In this adverbial use no particles attach. As a (pro)noun 모두 means 'everybody/everything' and takes particles: 모두가 이해했어요, 저는 선물을 모두에게 주었어요. However, in the plain pattern Subject – 모두 – Verb the object particle ~를 is normally dropped (저는 모두 먹고 싶어요), because 모두 is functioning adverbially there. When a group word precedes it, ~를/~가 are attached: 저는 가족 모두를 사랑해요, 학생 모두가 기숙사로 갔어요.

drills.translation: All the teachers are smart.
drills.hint: bare adverb meaning 'all', no particle

drills.translation: I want to eat everything.
drills.hint: 'everything' with the object particle dropped

drills.translation: Everybody understood.
drills.hint: 'everybody' marked as the subject

drills.translation: Everybody is going for a walk.
drills.hint: 'everybody' marked as the subject

drills.translation: I love all of my family.
drills.hint: 'all of them' marked as the object
drills.cell: object after a group word 모두 + ~를

drills.translation: I gave a present to everybody.
drills.hint: 'to everybody'

drills.translation: All of the students went to the dorm.
drills.hint: 'all of them' as the subject of the sentence

drills.translation: I understood everything.
drills.hint: 'everything' with no particle attached

drills.sentence: 그 배우는 짧은 연설로 관객 {{answer}} 감동시켰다.
drills.translation: That actor moved the entire audience with a short speech.
drills.hint: '전부, 다'를 뜻하는 집합 명사에 목적격 조사를 붙여 쓰세요.
drills.transliteration: geu baeuneun jjalbeun yeonseollo gwan-gaek ___ gamdongsikyeotda.
drills.cell: object after a group word 모두 + ~를

drills.sentence: 이 좋은 소식을 {{answer}} 빨리 알려 주세요.
drills.translation: Please tell this good news to everyone quickly.
drills.hint: Use the word meaning 'everyone/all' plus the dative particle ~에게 (to someone).
drills.transliteration: i joeun sosigeul ___ ppalli allyeo juseyo.

paradigm: object after a group word 모두 + ~를

points.title: Question word + ~나 (everywhere / every time / everyone)
points.function: Turn 어디, 언제, 누구 into 'everywhere', 'every time/always', 'everyone'.
points.explanation: Add ~나 to the question words 어디 (where), 언제 (when) and 누구 (who) to get 어디나 (everywhere), 언제나 (every time / always) and 누구나 (everyone). Particles are usually not added to these words.

drills.translation: I want to travel everywhere in Korea.
drills.hint: 'in all places', from the word for 'where'

drills.translation: Rice tastes the same everywhere.
drills.hint: 'in all places', from the word for 'where'

drills.translation: She comes late every time.
drills.hint: 'at all times', from the word for 'when'

drills.translation: I always wake up at the same time.
drills.hint: 'at all times', from the word for 'when'

drills.translation: Everybody likes Korea.
drills.hint: 'all people', from the word for 'who'

drills.translation: Everybody wants to see our baby.
drills.hint: 'all people', from the word for 'who'

drills.translation: We will go everywhere in South East Asia.
drills.hint: 'all places' word built on 어디

drills.translation: I always eat the same thing on the menu.
drills.hint: 'at all times' word built on 언제

drills.translation: Everybody knows that girl.
drills.hint: 'all people' word built on 누구

points.title: Question word + ~ㄴ가 (something / somewhere / sometime / somebody)
points.function: Turn 뭐, 어디, 언제, 누구 into 'something', 'somewhere', 'sometime', 'somebody'.
points.explanation: Add ~ㄴ가: 뭐 → 뭔가, 어디 → 어딘가, 언제 → 언젠가, 누구 → 누군가. Particle behaviour differs: subject/object particles are very often dropped after 뭔가 (뭔가(를) 먹고 싶어요); with 어딘가 you normally need ~에 or ~에서 — ~에 may be dropped but ~에서 should not be; ~에 is typically not attached to 언젠가, and ~까지/~부터 are not used with it; 누군가 freely takes particles (누군가가, 누군가의, 누군가와).

drills.translation: There is something on your back.
drills.hint: an unspecified thing, from the word for 'what'

drills.translation: I want to say something.
drills.hint: an unspecified thing, from the word for 'what'

drills.translation: I left my keys somewhere.
drills.hint: an unspecified place, from the word for 'where'

drills.translation: Blood is coming out of somewhere.
drills.hint: an unspecified place, from the word for 'where'

drills.translation: That day will come sometime.
drills.hint: an unspecified time, from the word for 'when'

drills.translation: I want to become a police officer someday.
drills.hint: an unspecified time, from the word for 'when'

drills.translation: Somebody is looking for you.
drills.hint: an unspecified person, from the word for 'who'

drills.translation: I found somebody's keys.
drills.hint: an unspecified person, from the word for 'who'

drills.translation: I feel something on my arm.
drills.hint: 'some thing', built on 뭐

drills.translation: I want to go somewhere on the holiday.
drills.hint: 'some place', built on 어디

drills.translation: Somebody lost their wallet.
drills.hint: 'some person', built on 누구

drills.translation: The clouds will clear sometime.
drills.hint: 'at some time', built on 언제

points.title: 어느 + noun (some / an ambiguous ___)
points.function: Refer to a vague, unspecified time or place, as in storytelling.
points.explanation: Besides its 'which' meaning, 어느 can be placed before a broad word of time or place to refer to it vaguely: 어느 날, 어느 밤, 어느 겨울, 어느 여름, 어느 마을, 어느 시장. This is typical of stories, poetry and news reports where the exact time or place need not be given — the Korean equivalent of 'a long time ago in a far-away land'.
points.culture_note: This is the register of fairy tales and news openings, similar to English 'one day…' or 'in a certain village…'.

drills.translation: One winter, all the flowers disappeared.
drills.hint: the vague determiner placed before a time word

drills.translation: Two babies were born in a certain village.
drills.hint: the vague determiner placed before a place word

drills.translation: One day a letter suddenly arrived from a friend.
drills.hint: the determiner that leaves the day unidentified — the same word as 'which', used vaguely

drills.translation: Long ago, in a certain country, there lived a king.
drills.hint: the determiner a fairy tale puts before the country so it is never named

drills.sentence: 언젠가 {{answer}} 작은 섬에서 조용히 살고 싶어요.
drills.translation: Someday I'd like to live quietly on some small island.
drills.hint: vague determiner opening the noun phrase — you have no particular island in mind
drills.transliteration: eonjenga {{answer}} jageun seomeseo joyonghi salgo sipeoyo.

drills.translation: One night the child did not come home.
drills.hint: narrative determiner before the word for night, leaving which night unspecified

drills.sentence: {{answer}} 도시에서 큰 사고가 났다는 뉴스를 봤어요.
drills.translation: I saw the news that a big accident had happened in some city.
drills.hint: the determiner a news report uses when the city is not being named
drills.transliteration: {{answer}} dosieseo keun sagoga natdaneun nyuseureul bwasseoyo.

points.title: 뭐 / 어디 / 누구 as 'something / somewhere / somebody'
points.function: Use bare question words to refer to an unspecified thing, place or person.
points.explanation: 뭐, 어디 and 누구 can be used without ~ㄴ가 to point to an ambiguous thing, place or person: 어디 갔어 = (she) went somewhere; 우리가 이미 뭐 먹었어요 = we already ate something; 나는 내일 누구 만날 거야 = tomorrow I'm meeting somebody. The same sentence can therefore be either a question word sentence or a yes/no question: 뭐 먹었어요? = 'What did you eat?' or 'Did you eat something?'. The difference is stress: stress the question word for the 'what/where/who' reading, and stress the verb for the 'something/somewhere/somebody' reading.

drills.translation: No, she went somewhere.
drills.hint: bare place question word used vaguely

drills.translation: We already ate something.
drills.hint: bare thing question word used vaguely

drills.translation: Tomorrow I'm going to meet somebody.
drills.hint: bare person question word used vaguely

drills.translation: I'd like to go somewhere for fun this weekend.
drills.hint: bare place word, no particle attached — the destination has not been decided

drills.translation: My older brother has been on the phone with somebody for a while.
drills.hint: bare person word carrying the 'with' particle — the other party goes unnamed

drills.translation: I think I left my bag somewhere.
drills.hint: bare place word standing in for a spot you cannot pin down

points.title: 아무나 / 아무도 (anybody / nobody)
points.function: Say 'anybody' in positive sentences and 'nobody' in negative sentences.
points.explanation: 아무 is a pronoun meaning 'any (person)'. With ~나 it forms 아무나 = 'anybody', used in positive sentences; with ~도 it forms 아무도 = 'nobody/not anybody', which requires a negative predicate (안, 못, ~지 않다, 없다). Because ~나 and ~도 are themselves particles, ~는/~가/~를 are not stacked on top of them. If 아무 has another role in the sentence, a particle goes before ~나/~도 — most often 'to' (~에게/~한테) or 'with' (~와/~하고): 아무에게나, 아무하고나, 아무에게도, 아무하고도. Simple rule for beginners: 아무나 for sentences that end positively, 아무도 for sentences that end negatively.

drills.translation: Anybody would like that book.
drills.hint: 'any person at all' in a positive sentence

drills.sentence: 이렇게 좋은 학교에서는 {{answer}} 공부를 잘 할 거예요.
drills.translation: At such a good school anybody would study well.
drills.hint: 'any person at all' in a positive sentence
drills.transliteration: ireoke joeun hakgyoeseoneun ___ gongbureul jal hal geoyeyo.

drills.translation: There is nobody at home.
drills.hint: 'not one person' — requires a negative ending

drills.translation: Nobody likes me.
drills.hint: 'not one person' — requires a negative ending

drills.translation: I want to give this present to anybody.
drills.hint: 'to any person at all', positive

drills.translation: I didn't say that to anybody.
drills.hint: 'to not one person', negative

drills.translation: I want to play soccer with anybody.
drills.hint: 'with any person at all', positive

drills.translation: I don't want to talk with anybody.
drills.hint: 'with not one person', negative

drills.translation: I didn't see anybody.
drills.hint: the 'not one person' form used with a negative verb

drills.translation: I want to go out with anybody.
drills.hint: 'with any person at all', using the 와 form

drills.translation: Anybody can do this job.
drills.hint: 'any person at all' in a positive sentence

drills.sentence: 이런 중요한 서류를 {{answer}} 맡기면 안 됩니다.
drills.translation: You must not entrust such important documents to just anyone.
drills.hint: Use the indefinite pronoun meaning 'anyone' with the dative particle plus the '-나' ending, giving the sense 'to just anybody'.
drills.transliteration: ireon jungyohan seoryureul ___ matgimyeon an doemnida.

drills.translation: Don't tell this secret to anyone.
drills.hint: Use the dative 'to' form of '아무' plus the particle that pairs with negatives (here, a prohibition).

drills.sentence: 우리 강아지는 성격이 좋아서 {{answer}} 잘 놀아요.
drills.translation: Our puppy has a good temperament, so it plays well with anyone.
drills.hint: '누구든 상관없이 함께'라는 뜻으로, 부정 대명사에 '와/과' 대신 쓰는 구어체 조사와 '나'를 붙인 긍정형
drills.transliteration: uri gangajineun seonggyeogi joaseo ___ jal norayo.

drills.sentence: 그는 요즘 기분이 안 좋아서 {{answer}} 말을 하지 않아요.
drills.translation: He's in a bad mood these days, so he doesn't talk with anyone.
drills.hint: 부정문에서 '어떤 사람과도 (전혀)'라는 뜻을 나타내는 표현을 쓰세요.
drills.transliteration: geuneun yojeum gibuni an joaseo ___ mareul haji anayo.

points.title: 아무 + 거/데/때 + ~나 (anything / anywhere / anytime)
points.function: Say 'anything', 'anywhere', 'anytime' by putting 아무 before a general noun.
points.explanation: 아무 can also stand before a general thing/place/time noun: 거 (short for 것, 'thing'), 데 ('place'), 때 ('time'). With ~나 attached the speaker shows the thing/place/time is not a specific one: 아무 거나 (anything), 아무 데나 (anywhere), 아무 때나 (anytime, = 언제든지). With 데, ~에 is omitted before ~나, but if the verb requires ~에서, it is inserted before ~나 (아무 데서나). The negative counterparts are 아무 것도 (nothing) and 아무 데도 (nowhere), which need a negative predicate.

drills.translation: I want to eat anything (I'd eat anything).
drills.hint: 'any thing at all', positive

drills.translation: I want to go anywhere (I'd go anywhere).
drills.hint: 'any place at all', positive

drills.translation: Anytime is good.
drills.hint: 'any time at all', positive

drills.translation: I didn't eat anything today.
drills.hint: 'not one thing', needs a negative verb

drills.translation: I didn't go anywhere yesterday.
drills.hint: 'not one place', needs a negative verb

drills.translation: It's fine for me to eat anything.
drills.hint: 'any thing at all', positive form

drills.translation: Please sit anywhere.
drills.hint: 'any place at all', positive form

drills.translation: I didn't eat anything.
drills.hint: 'not one thing', negative form

drills.translation: If you're hungry, you can take anything out of the fridge and eat it.
drills.hint: 자유 선택을 나타내는 표현: '무엇이든 상관없다'는 뜻으로, '아무'에 사물을 가리키는 말과 조사 '-나'가 붙은 형태 (긍정문에 쓰임).

drills.sentence: 이 카페는 24시간 문을 열어서 {{answer}} 들를 수 있어요.
drills.translation: This cafe is open 24 hours, so you can drop by anytime.
drills.hint: Use the indefinite time expression meaning '언제든지' (at any time you like).
drills.transliteration: i kapeneun isipsasigan muneul yeoreoseo ___ deulleul su isseoyo.

drills.sentence: 배가 너무 불러서 지금은 {{answer}} 먹고 싶지 않아요.
drills.translation: I'm so full that I don't want to eat anything right now.

points.title: 아무 + ~나 / ~도 (any… / none…)
points.function: Say 'any(one/thing/where)' or, with a negative verb, 'nobody/nothing/nowhere'.
points.explanation: 아무 is placed before a noun. Adding ~나 to that noun gives the meaning 'any …' (아무나 = anybody, 아무 거나 = anything, 아무 데나 = anywhere, 아무 때나 = anytime). Replacing ~나 with ~도 and using a negative predicate gives 'nobody / nothing / nowhere' (아무도, 아무 것도, 아무 데도). The location form depends on the verb: with movement verbs (가다) that take ~에 you use 아무 데나 / 아무 데도, while with verbs describing an action done at a place (먹다), which take ~에서, you use 아무 데서나. Nouns other than 거/데/때 may follow 아무 (아무 버스나, 아무 말도, 아무 관계도), but 거, 데 and 때 are by far the most common.

points.title: ~마다 (each / every)
points.function: Attach to a noun to say 'each' or 'every' one of it.
points.explanation: ~마다 means 'each' and is attached directly to the end of a noun with no space: 날마다 (each day), 학생마다 (each student), 금요일마다 (every Friday), 30분마다 (every 30 minutes). It differs subtly from 모든, which precedes the noun and means 'every/all': 모든 학생 = 'every student' as a group, 학생마다 = 'each individual student'.

points.title: ~에 vs ~에서 with places
points.function: Choose the right place particle depending on the verb.
points.explanation: ~에 marks a destination and is used with movement verbs such as 가다 and 오다. ~에서 marks the location where an action takes place and is used with action verbs such as 먹다 or 공부하다. The same place noun therefore takes a different particle depending on the verb.

drills.hint: destination particle used with verbs of going

drills.translation: Come to my house tomorrow.

drills.translation: I didn't go to work today.
